A continuation of the account: the story of the church, from Pentecost onward.

For forty days after He rose, the Lord came and went among us, and they were the strangest and sweetest days of my life. He would be there when the doors were shut, and gone again, and then walking on a beach at dawn cooking fish over a fire of coals. He ate with us to prove He was no phantom; I saw Him take a piece of broiled fish and a bit of honeycomb and eat it before our eyes, and I touched the place in His side where the spear had gone in. He was the same and not the same—the very Man we had followed three years on the dusty roads of Galilee, and yet risen into a life that death could no longer touch. He opened the Scriptures to us in those days as He had on the Emmaus road, showing us from Moses and the Prophets and the Psalms how the Christ had to suffer and rise, until the whole of our holy writings seemed to turn like a face toward Him.

On the last of those days He led us out toward Bethany, to the Mount of Olives, and we asked Him—still half dreaming of thrones and armies—whether He would now restore the kingdom to Israel. He answered that it was not for us to know the times the Father had fixed by His own authority, but that we would receive power when the Holy Spirit came upon us, and would be His witnesses in Jerusalem, in all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth. I have come to see that those few words were the whole map of everything that followed—Jerusalem first, then the despised Samaritans, then the very ends of the earth, the gospel rolling outward in ever-widening circles until it reached the nations. He was telling us, before it began, how far His salvation meant to travel.

And then, while He was blessing us, with His hands still lifted over our heads, He was taken up, and a cloud received Him out of our sight. We stood staring into the sky long after He was gone, our necks craned, our hearts torn between joy and bereavement, until two men in white robes stood beside us and said, "Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into heaven? This Jesus, who was taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same way as you saw Him go." It was a promise wrapped in a gentle rebuke: He had not abandoned us, and there was work to do, and He would come again. So we turned from the empty sky and went down the hill back into the city, carrying His blessing and His promise, to wait for the power He had pledged.

I have wondered, in the long years since, why He stayed those forty days at all, coming and going among us, rather than ascending straight from the empty tomb. I think now it was for our sakes, that we might be left in no doubt. He gave us, He said, many proofs that He was alive—the wounds touched, the fish eaten, the Scriptures opened—so that when the time came to give our testimony, even to die for it, we would not be testifying to a hope or a feeling or a dream, but to a thing we had seen and handled. A man may be mistaken about a vision in the night; he is not mistaken about the friend who broke bread with him on a hillside at dawn. The Lord knew that the witness He was about to scatter across the world would be hated and doubted and put to the sword, and He grounded it, before He left, in forty days of plain and unanswerable fact.

We climbed the stairs to the upper room where we had been staying—the same kind of low, lamp-lit chamber where He had broken bread and washed our feet, perhaps the very one. We were eleven of the chosen now, with the women who had followed Him, and Mary His mother, and His brothers, who had mocked Him once and worshiped Him now, for they too had met Him risen. There is a particular bond among people who have wept the same tears and seen the same impossible morning, and we had it. We had no power of our own yet, only a promise; and so we did the one thing that people with empty hands can do, which is to pray, and we gave ourselves to it day after day, the prayers rising in that small room like the first smoke of an offering.

In those days Peter stood up among the brothers, about a hundred and twenty of us in all. He was changed from the man who had cursed and sworn by the fire that he never knew the Lord; the threefold restoration on the beach had put a new kind of steel in him, the gentle, unbreakable steel that comes not from confidence in oneself but from having been forgiven much and knowing it. He spoke of Judas, who had walked with us and seen everything and sold the Lord for silver, and who had gone to his own terrible end, the field bought with his blood-money standing empty to this day. The Scripture had foretold it, Peter said, and had said too that another should take his office of oversight.

So they put forward two men who had been with us the whole way, from the baptism of John until the day the Lord was taken up—Joseph called Barsabbas, and Matthias. And we prayed, asking the Lord who knows all hearts to show which one He had chosen, and we cast lots, and the lot fell to Matthias, and he was numbered with the eleven apostles. I have thought often about that quiet morning. Before the Spirit had even fallen, before the first sermon was preached, the Lord was already mending what the betrayal had torn, filling the empty place at the table, restoring the broken number of the witnesses to its wholeness. It was as if He wished to show us from the very start that no man's treachery, not even Judas's, could thwart the purpose of God or leave a permanent wound in His work. The traitor had fallen away; the testimony stood whole. And so, made complete again, we settled back to wait for the thing He had promised would come upon us.

I have come to love that quiet, hidden time of waiting and prayer, though we did not love it then, for we were impatient for the power He had promised. But I see now that the Lord does much of His deepest work in His people in just such hidden seasons, when nothing seems to be happening and we are tempted to think ourselves forgotten. We were being made ready. The same men who would soon stand before thousands were first shut up together in an upper room with nothing to do but pray and wait and learn to depend on a promise. I have noticed that He nearly always brings His servants through such a wilderness of waiting before He uses them greatly, as He led Moses to the back of the desert and Paul into Arabia and His own Son into the wilderness; for power that is not first born in prayer and dependence will only puff a man up and destroy him.

When the day of Pentecost came, we were all together in one place. It was the feast of weeks, the fiftieth day after the Passover when He had died as the true Lamb, the feast when our people brought the firstfruits of the wheat harvest and remembered the giving of the law on Sinai. The city was swollen again with pilgrims from every land under heaven, the streets a river of languages, the air thick with the smell of dust and bread and the smoke of the altar. The morning had begun like any other—the ordinary noises of a waking city below the window, the ordinary light slanting across the floor—and then, all at once, it was not ordinary at all.

There came a sound from heaven like a mighty rushing wind, and it filled the whole house where we were sitting. I felt it before I understood it, a roaring and a pressure that was not wind, for not a cup was stirred on the table and not a hair moved on my head, and yet the sound was everywhere, inside us and around us. Then there appeared to us tongues as of fire, dividing and resting on each one of us. I looked at the faces of my companions and saw the small flames standing above them, steady and bright, and I knew without being told that the Helper He had promised in the upper room had come at last—that He had kept His word and had not left us as orphans. We were all filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in other tongues as the Spirit gave us utterance. I heard my own mouth forming words I had never learned, and all around me the others were doing the same, a flood of speech that was not babble but a hundred clear languages.

The sound drew a crowd in the street below, and they were bewildered, because every man heard us declaring the mighty works of God in the tongue of his own birth—Parthians and Medes and Elamites, dwellers in Mesopotamia and Judea and Cappadocia, men from Pontus and Asia, from Phrygia and Egypt and the parts of Libya near Cyrene, visitors from Rome, Cretans and Arabs, each one hearing his mother's language on the lips of Galileans. Some were amazed and perplexed, asking one another what it could mean. Others sneered and said we were filled with new wine, though it was only the third hour of the morning. I have pondered long why He poured out His Spirit in just this way, scattering the gospel into so many tongues in a single hour. At Babel, long ago, God had confused the speech of proud men building a tower to heaven and scattered them across the earth; now, at Pentecost, He gave many tongues to humble men and began to gather the scattered nations back in. It was the Savior of the world keeping the word I had first heard from Samaritans at a well, that He had not come for one people only. The Spirit who fell on us that morning was nothing less than the very life of the risen Christ, applied at last to our own hearts and poured out through our mouths; everything He had purchased on the cross was now being pressed into us and through us, out toward the ends of the earth. We had been a frightened huddle behind locked doors; in one morning we became a fire that could not be hidden.

I have thought, too, on the strangeness of the fire that did not burn. The tongues rested on each of us and we were not consumed, and I remembered Moses at the bush that flamed and was not eaten away, and the pillar of fire that had gone before our fathers in the wilderness. God had always come to His people in fire—but that fire had kept men at a distance, fencing the mountain, warning them not to draw near lest they die. Now the fire came down and sat gently upon ordinary heads, upon fishermen and former tax collectors and women, and did not destroy them but filled them. The God who had once been hidden behind smoke and trembling on Sinai had come, through the torn veil, to dwell in His people themselves. That, I have come to see, is what the whole gospel had been moving toward: not a God who keeps us at the foot of the mountain, but a God who makes His home in us.

Then Peter stood up with the eleven, lifted his voice, and addressed the crowd, and I stood near him and watched the fisherman become a herald. He told them plainly that we were not drunk, as they supposed, for it was but the third hour of the day, but that this was what the prophet Joel had spoken—that in the last days God would pour out His Spirit on all flesh, on sons and daughters, on young and old, on menservants and maidservants, and that whoever called on the name of the Lord would be saved. And then he did a thing of breathtaking boldness: he preached Jesus to the very city that had killed Him, scarcely fifty days after the deed.

He spoke of Jesus of Nazareth, a man attested by God with mighty works and wonders and signs that God did through Him in their midst, as they themselves knew. And he did not soften the charge: "This Jesus, delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, you crucified and killed by the hands of lawless men." But God raised Him up, Peter declared, loosing the pangs of death, because it was not possible for death to hold Him. He held up the words of David, who had written that God would not abandon His Holy One to corruption—and David, Peter reminded them, was dead and buried, his tomb still among them, so he had spoken not of himself but of the Christ who would rise. I marveled, listening, at how Peter held two truths together in a single breath, the very two I had wrestled so hard to hold myself. The cross was the most wicked thing that men had ever done—and it was the very thing God had planned before the foundation of the world for our salvation. Human malice and divine mercy had met at Golgotha and done the same deed, the blackest sin and the deepest grace folded into one act, and neither cancelled the other. This crucified Jesus, now risen and exalted to the right hand of God and having poured out the Spirit they now saw and heard, God had made both Lord and Christ.

When the people heard this, they were cut to the heart, and they cried out, "Brothers, what shall we do?" I have never forgotten the answer, for it was the whole of what I had learned, now offered freely to the very hands that had driven the nails: "Repent and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of your sins, and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit. For the promise is for you and for your children and for all who are far off, everyone whom the Lord our God calls to Himself." There was no debt too great to be forgiven, not even the blood of the Son of God; the men who had shouted "Crucify Him" not seven weeks before were now being offered the very forgiveness that His blood had bought. And he kept exhorting them, urging them to be saved from that crooked generation. That day about three thousand souls received his word and were baptized. I watched them go down into the water, group after group, and I thought of John standing in the Jordan long ago crying, "Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world," and I understood that the taking-away had now begun in earnest, that the harvest the Lamb had died to gather was coming in by the thousands.

And I have marveled since at where Peter began. He did not begin with himself, nor with us, nor even with the wonder the crowd had just witnessed; he began with the Scriptures, with Joel and with David, showing that nothing happening before their eyes was new or strange, but the very thing the prophets had foretold for the last days. This is how the Lord had taught us to read, on the Emmaus road and in the upper room—that all the Scriptures spoke of Him. And so the church was born not on the strength of a spectacle but on the foundation of the written word, rightly opened; for a faith built on signs alone will fail when the signs fade, but a faith built on the word of God endures, because that word does not pass away.

Those first days had a brightness to them that I can scarcely describe to anyone who was not there. We who believed were together and held all things in common, and those who had lands or houses sold them and brought the proceeds to be laid at the apostles' feet and distributed to any who had need. No one called what he owned his own. Day by day we devoted ourselves to four things—the apostles' teaching, the fellowship, the breaking of bread, and the prayers—gathering in the Temple courts in the great open daylight and then in one another's homes as the lamps were lit. We ate together with glad and generous hearts, and the smell of those shared meals, the cheap bread and oil and thin wine of poor men passed from hand to hand, still comes back to me across all these years as the very smell of joy. Awe came upon every soul, for many wonders and signs were being done through the apostles, and a holy gladness lay over the whole company like morning light.

I have come to understand that this open-handedness was not a rule we laid upon ourselves, nor some discipline we gritted our teeth to keep; it was simply the overflow of grace. People who have been forgiven a debt they could never pay cannot easily go on clutching their coins; the mercy that has been poured into them keeps spilling out toward whoever stands near. We had received everything as a gift, and so we found we could hold everything as a gift, with open hands. It was the parable of the unforgiving servant turned right side out at last—a whole community of people who knew the size of what they had been forgiven, and so could not bear to let a brother go hungry while they had bread. And the Lord added to our number day by day those who were being saved, until the little band that had hidden behind locked doors had become a thronging multitude in the heart of the city that had crucified its King.

I have grown old enough now to know how rare and precious those days were, and how soon the first bloom of a thing can fade if it is not guarded. But I have also learned that the four things to which we gave ourselves in that first season are the very things that keep a church alive in every season: the apostles' teaching, that we not drift from the truth; the fellowship, that we not grow cold and solitary; the breaking of bread, that we never forget the body broken and the blood poured out for us; and the prayers, that we lean always on God and not on ourselves. Where these four are kept, the life remains; where any of them is let go, the life begins to ebb, however much else may be busy and impressive. The Lord builds His church not on great schemes but on these small, faithful, daily things.

One afternoon Peter and John went up to the Temple at the hour of prayer, the ninth hour, and I went up with them. At the gate called Beautiful sat a man lame from his mother's womb, carried there and laid down each day to beg from those entering the Temple, as he had been laid for more than forty years. He saw us about to go in and asked us for alms, his hand out, his eyes already sliding past us to the next pilgrim, expecting at best a coin. Peter fixed his gaze on him, and so did John, and said, "Look at us." So he looked, expecting to receive something from them. And Peter said, "I have no silver and gold, but what I do have I give to you. In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, rise up and walk." And he took him by the right hand and raised him up, and immediately his feet and ankles were made strong. He leaped up and stood and began to walk, and then to leap, and he went into the Temple with us, walking and leaping and praising God. I had seen the Lord Himself raise such men with a word; now I saw that same power flow through Peter's calloused hand—not Peter's power, but the Lord's, working through His name.

All the people came running together to us in astonishment, in the portico called Solomon's. But Peter would not let them stare at us as though we had done this by our own power or our own piety. "Why do you wonder at this," he said, "or why do you stare at us, as though by our own power or godliness we have made him walk?" He preached Jesus to them again—the Author of life, whom they had denied and killed, asking for a murderer to be released instead, and whom God had raised from the dead. It was faith in the name of Jesus, Peter said, that had made this man strong, whom they saw and knew. "Repent therefore, and turn back, that your sins may be blotted out." It struck me freshly, watching the healed man cling to Peter and John in the portico, that everything still ran through the name—not through any goodness in the one healed, who had only begged, not through any holiness in the ones who spoke, who were unlearned fishermen, but through the name of the crucified and risen One alone. The lame man's leaping feet were themselves a sermon written in flesh: this is what the salvation of God does to a man who could never once stand on his own. It lifts him up by a hand he did not deserve, and sets him leaping into the house of God.

I have often returned, in my mind, to the look on that man's face. He had asked for a coin, expecting nothing more, having asked for coins at that gate every day for longer than I had been alive; and he received instead his feet, his ankles, his whole life made new. It has seemed to me a parable of how God so often answers us—we come to Him asking for some small mercy, some easing of our circumstances, a little silver to get us through the day, and He gives us instead the thing we never thought to ask for and could never have imagined, Himself and His salvation, and sends us leaping into His house. We ask for coins; He gives us sons' inheritance. I have learned not to be disappointed when He withholds the small thing I begged for, for it is often because His hand is full of something far greater.

While we were still speaking to the people, the priests and the captain of the Temple guard and the Sadducees came upon us, greatly annoyed that we were teaching the people and proclaiming in Jesus the resurrection from the dead—the very doctrine the Sadducees denied. They arrested Peter and John and held them overnight, for it was already evening. But many of those who had heard the word believed, and the number of the men came to about five thousand. The seed scattered in that one sermon was already a harvest.

The next day the rulers and elders and scribes gathered in Jerusalem—Annas the high priest was there, and Caiaphas, the very men who had condemned the Lord to death not two months before—and they set Peter and John in their midst and demanded, "By what power or by what name did you do this?" Then Peter, filled with the Holy Spirit, said the thing that I have carried in my heart ever since as the plainest summary of the gospel that I know. He told them the lame man stood before them well by the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, whom they had crucified and God had raised. "This Jesus," he said, "is the stone that was rejected by you, the builders, which has become the cornerstone. And there is salvation in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved." No other name. Not Moses, not the Temple in whose courts they stood, not the law, not their descent from Abraham, not any goodness of our own—only the name they had tried to silence by killing the One who bore it. The rulers saw the boldness of Peter and John and perceived that they were uneducated, common men, and they were astonished, and they recognized that they had been with Jesus. I have found that to be true ever since: being with Him leaves a mark that no schooling can give and no threat can erase, a boldness that does not come from the man but from the One who stands with him.

They could find nothing to say against it, for the man who had been healed was standing right there beside us, and they could not deny the miracle. So they conferred and then charged us to speak no more at all in that name, and threatened us, and let us go, finding no way to punish us because of the people, who were all glorifying God. But when Peter and John were released and came to us and reported what the chief priests and elders had said, we did not pray for safety. We lifted our voices together to God and prayed for boldness—that He would look upon their threats and grant His servants to continue to speak His word with all boldness, while He stretched out His hand to heal, and signs and wonders were performed through the name of His holy servant Jesus. And when we had prayed, the place in which we were gathered together was shaken, and we were all filled afresh with the Holy Spirit and went on speaking the word of God with boldness. I have noticed, across all the years since, that He does not often take the danger away. He gives instead the courage to walk straight into it, which is the better gift by far, for it teaches us to lean on Him and not on calm circumstances, and it leaves us, when the danger has passed, knowing that it was He and not our own nerve who carried us through.

I have noticed, looking back over the whole of it, how the council kept making the same mistake, again and again, that it had made with the Lord. They had supposed that by killing Jesus they would be rid of Him and of this troublesome teaching; and within weeks His followers were filling the very courts where He had been condemned, and the man they had crucified was being preached as Lord by the thousands. Now they thought that by threatening two unlearned fishermen they could stop the word. But you cannot threaten men into silence when they have seen the dead rise; you cannot frighten away those who no longer fear death. The council had power over bodies and prisons and even over life, and it availed them nothing, because the thing they were fighting was not a movement of men but the purpose of God, and against that no scheme of the rulers of this age has ever prevailed.

The whole company of those who believed were of one heart and soul, and no one said that any of his possessions was his own, but they had everything in common. Great grace was upon us all, and there was not a needy person among us, for as many as owned lands or houses sold them and laid the proceeds at the apostles' feet, to be distributed as any had need. Among them was a Levite from Cyprus named Joseph, whom the apostles called Barnabas, which means son of encouragement; he sold a field he owned and laid the money at the apostles' feet, and many did likewise, gladly, freely, in the joy of the grace that had been poured into them.

But a man named Ananias, with the knowledge of his wife Sapphira, sold a piece of property and kept back for himself part of the proceeds, and brought only a portion and laid it at the apostles' feet, while pretending that it was the whole. Peter said, "Ananias, why has Satan filled your heart to lie to the Holy Spirit and to keep back for yourself part of the proceeds of the land? While it remained unsold, did it not remain your own? And after it was sold, was it not at your disposal? Why is it that you have contrived this deed in your heart? You have not lied to men but to God." And when Ananias heard these words, he fell down and breathed his last. About three hours later his wife came in, not knowing what had happened, and told the same lie, and she too fell down and died at Peter's feet. And great fear came upon the whole church and upon all who heard of it.

That day frightened me, and I have pondered it for many years since. The sin was not that they kept back some of their money, for Peter said plainly that the field had been theirs to sell or keep, and the money theirs to give or withhold. The sin was the lie—the pretense of a holiness they did not have, the attempt to purchase a reputation for generosity within the very community that lived by free grace, to be admired as Barnabas was admired, while secretly hedging their hearts. It was the leaven of the Pharisees, the old hypocrisy the Lord had warned against, creeping back into the house of the forgiven. And I came to understand a thing that has steadied and sobered me ever since: that the God who is tender beyond all measure toward the sinner who comes to Him empty-handed, with nothing to plead but mercy, is severe toward the pretense that imagines it can deceive Him while trading on His grace. The same mercy that had received tax collectors and harlots and a dying thief would not be mocked by play-acting at devotion. It made me resolve to come to Him always exactly as I was, with no pretense and no performance, for the only ones He turns away are those who will not admit that they need Him.

I have thought much, over the years, about why this severe judgment came at the very dawn of the church, when grace was so freshly and freely flowing. And I have come to believe it was a mercy, however terrible—a warning set up at the threshold, that we might know forever what kind of God we were dealing with. He is not mocked, and He will not be used. The hypocrisy of Ananias, if it had been let pass, would have spread through the young church like the leaven the Lord had warned us against, until the community of the forgiven became another den of pretenders, every man performing a holiness he did not have. The same God who runs to embrace the returning prodigal will not be flattered by the elder brother's show of duty. And so I learned to fear Him rightly—not with the terror of a slave, but with the awe of a son who knows that the Father who loves him also sees straight through him, and loves him far too much to let him live a lie.

Many signs and wonders were regularly done among the people by the hands of the apostles, and we were all together in Solomon's portico. None of the rest dared join us out of fear, yet the people held us in high esteem, and more than ever believers were added to the Lord, multitudes of both men and women, so that they even carried the sick out into the streets and laid them on cots and mats, that as Peter came by at least his shadow might fall on some of them. The people gathered also from the towns around Jerusalem, bringing the sick and those afflicted with unclean spirits, and they were all healed. The mercy that had once flowed from the hem of the Lord's garment in Galilee was flowing still, now through the shadow of a fisherman, and not one who came was turned away.

Then the high priest rose up, and all who were with him, the party of the Sadducees, and filled with jealousy they arrested the apostles and put them in the public prison. But during the night an angel of the Lord opened the prison doors and brought them out and said, "Go and stand in the Temple and speak to the people all the words of this Life." So at daybreak they entered the Temple and began to teach. When the council sent to the prison to have them brought, the officers found it securely locked and the guards standing at the doors, but no one inside; and word came that the men they had jailed were standing in the Temple teaching the people. Brought before the council again, and reminded that they had been strictly charged not to teach in this name, Peter and the apostles answered, "We must obey God rather than men. The God of our fathers raised Jesus, whom you killed by hanging Him on a tree. God exalted Him at His right hand as Leader and Savior, to give repentance to Israel and forgiveness of sins."

When the council heard this they were enraged and wanted to kill them. But a Pharisee named Gamaliel, a teacher of the law held in honor by all the people, stood up and counseled caution. He recalled others who had risen up claiming to be somebody and had come to nothing once they were killed and their followers scattered. "So in the present case," he said, "keep away from these men and let them alone, for if this plan or this undertaking is of man, it will fail; but if it is of God, you will not be able to overthrow them. You might even be found opposing God." They took his advice, and after beating the apostles and charging them again to speak no more in the name of Jesus, they let them go. And the apostles left the presence of the council rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer dishonor for the name. I marveled at that joy when I heard it—men walking away from a public flogging glad, because they had been allowed to bear a little of what He had borne for them. The Master had said long before that whoever lost his life for His sake would find it, that those persecuted for His name should rejoice and be glad; and here it was, happening before my eyes. Every day, in the Temple and from house to house, they did not cease teaching and preaching that the Christ is Jesus.

It was a strange new thing in the world, this gladness in suffering, and I do not think any of us could have manufactured it. We had not been brave men. We had fled in the garden; I myself had stayed at a distance through much of His trial; Peter had denied Him to a servant girl. And now here were these same men, walking out of a flogging with their backs torn and bleeding, rejoicing—not gritting their teeth and enduring, but rejoicing—that they had been counted worthy to suffer dishonor for the name. The only thing that can account for such a change is the resurrection, and the Spirit poured out from the risen Lord. Cowards do not become martyrs by trying harder. They become martyrs when they have seen, with their own eyes, that the grave is empty and that the One who conquered death is with them.

As the disciples were increasing in number, a complaint arose, and it was the kind of complaint that can quietly poison a young and joyful thing if it is not met with wisdom and love. The Greek-speaking believers, the Hellenists, murmured against the Hebrews, because their widows were being neglected in the daily distribution of food, while the Hebrew widows were cared for. It was a small and practical matter on its face—who would see to it that bread reached the table of a poor foreign widow with no man to provide for her—and yet the unity of the body hung on it.

So the twelve summoned the full number of the disciples and said it was not right that they should give up preaching the word of God to wait on tables, and they bade us pick out from among ourselves seven men of good repute, full of the Spirit and of wisdom, whom they would appoint to this duty, that the apostles might devote themselves to prayer and to the ministry of the word. What they said pleased the whole gathering, and we chose Stephen, a man full of faith and of the Holy Spirit, and Philip, and five others, and set them before the apostles, who prayed and laid their hands on them. And the word of God continued to increase, and the number of the disciples multiplied greatly in Jerusalem, and a great many of the priests became obedient to the faith.

It seemed a small thing, the choosing of seven men to carry bread to widows, and yet I have come to see deep wisdom in it. The Lord had girded Himself with a towel and washed our feet to teach us that greatness in His kingdom is service; now the body He was building was learning the same lesson, taking pains that its weakest and most overlooked members—the widows, the foreigners, those with no voice and no advocate—should not be neglected. A church that had been saved by sheer mercy could not help but be marked by mercy, down to the daily bread on a forgotten widow's table. And I noticed something I have seen many times since: that when this care was rightly ordered, when love was given its proper place and the word its proper freedom, the gospel ran all the faster, and even priests who had served in the Temple bowed their heads to the crucified Christ. Mercy makes room for truth to run.

I have noticed, too, how the Lord turns even our complaints and shortfalls into the means of His grace. The neglect of the widows was a real failure, and it might have festered into bitterness and division between the Greek-speaking believers and the Hebrews; instead, in the hands of wise and humble men, it became the occasion for the church to learn to share its burdens and to set apart servants for the care of the weak. And from among those seven servants chosen merely to wait on tables came Stephen, the first martyr, and Philip, the evangelist who would carry the gospel to Samaria and to the Ethiopian. The Lord raised up His mightiest instruments from the lowliest service. I have learned never to despise the small and practical tasks of love, the carrying of bread to a forgotten widow, for it is often in such humble service that He prepares His servants for greater things, and it is always such service that adorns the gospel and lets the word run free.

Stephen, full of grace and power, did great wonders and signs among the people. But some of the men of the synagogue of the Freedmen rose up and disputed with him, and they could not withstand the wisdom and the Spirit with which he spoke. So, as they had done with the Lord, they secretly stirred up men to bring false charges, claiming he spoke blasphemous words against Moses and against God, against the holy place and the law. They seized him and brought him before the council and set up false witnesses, and all who sat in the council, gazing at him, saw that his face was like the face of an angel.

Then the high priest asked if these things were so, and Stephen answered with the whole long story of our people—Abraham called out from his country, Joseph sold by his brothers and yet made their savior, Moses rejected by the very people he came to deliver, the tabernacle and the Temple, the prophets persecuted one after another. And he showed how at every turn our fathers had resisted the Holy Spirit and rejected the deliverers God sent them, until at last they had betrayed and murdered the Righteous One Himself, of whom the prophets had foretold. "You stiff-necked people," he cried at the end, "uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit. As your fathers did, so do you." They were enraged and ground their teeth at him. But Stephen, full of the Holy Spirit, gazed into heaven and saw the glory of God, and Jesus standing at the right hand of God. "Behold," he said, "I see the heavens opened, and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God." At that they cried out with a loud voice, stopped their ears, and rushed together at him. They cast him out of the city and stoned him, and the witnesses laid down their garments at the feet of a young man named Saul. And as they were stoning him, Stephen called out, "Lord Jesus, receive my spirit." And falling to his knees, he cried with a loud voice, "Lord, do not hold this sin against them." And when he had said this, he fell asleep.

I was not there to see it with my own eyes, but those who were could not stop telling it, and every detail pierced me to the heart. For I had stood at the foot of another execution and heard another voice pray, "Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do," and then commit His spirit into His Father's hands. And now here was Stephen, the first of us to follow the Master all the way into death, dying in the very shape and image of his Lord—seeing heaven opened, as Nathanael had been promised on the first day he met Jesus that he would; beholding the Son of Man not seated on His throne but standing, as if the risen Christ had risen even from His seat in glory to receive His faithful servant home and to bear witness for him. Stephen committed his spirit to Jesus as Jesus had committed His to the Father, and forgave his murderers as Jesus had forgiven His. I understood then a thing I had not fully grasped before: that salvation does not only rescue us from death and hell; it remakes us into the very likeness of the One who saved us, until even our dying comes to look like His. And I saw, too, that the blood of the Lord, far from being avenged on those who shed it, was still pleading mercy for sinners through the lips of a dying man—for surely among the men who heard Stephen pray for their forgiveness, watching the coats at their feet, stood the very Saul whom that prayer would, before long, lay hold of and make new.

I have thought, too, of the young man at whose feet the witnesses laid their cloaks, watching it all with approval—Saul of Tarsus. He heard every word of Stephen's defense; he saw the face like an angel's; he heard the prayer for the forgiveness of the very men casting the stones, and surely that prayer was offered for him among them. And I have wondered whether the memory of that day did not go down into Saul like a seed buried in hard ground, to lie there through all his raging until the light on the Damascus road brought it to life. Stephen could not have known, as the stones struck him, that he was praying for the man who would carry the gospel to the ends of the earth. But the Lord knew. And it has taught me never to think any testimony wasted, even the testimony of a dying man before his murderers, for we cannot see what seed is taking root in the heart of the one who seems most set against us.

And Saul approved of his execution. On that day a great persecution broke out against the church in Jerusalem, and we were all scattered throughout the regions of Judea and Samaria, except the apostles, who remained. Devout men buried Stephen and made great lamentation over him. But Saul was ravaging the church, entering house after house, and dragging off men and women alike and committing them to prison. The huddle that the Spirit had set ablaze at Pentecost was now driven out of the city and scattered across the land. And yet, as I watched the believers flee with what little they could carry, I began to see a thing I could not have seen in the moment of grief: that the scattering itself was the sowing. Those who were scattered went about preaching the word wherever they went, so that the very persecution meant to stamp out the gospel only flung its seed into a hundred towns where it had never been heard. What our enemies intended for our destruction, God was bending into the spread of His word, exactly as He had once bent the cross itself.

Philip, one of the seven, went down to a city of Samaria and proclaimed to them the Christ. The crowds with one accord paid attention to what he said, hearing him and seeing the signs he did, for unclean spirits came out of many who were possessed, crying with a loud voice, and many who were paralyzed or lame were healed. And there was much joy in that city. I thought again of the woman at the well in those same Samaritan hills, the first soul to whom the Lord had told plainly who He was, and of how He had said the hour was coming when men would worship the Father neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem but in spirit and in truth. Now it was coming to pass before our eyes; the well was overflowing, and a people we had been raised to despise was drinking the living water with joy.

There was in that city a man named Simon, who had practiced magic and amazed the people, claiming to be somebody great, so that they called him the great power of God. Even he believed and was baptized and followed Philip, astonished at the signs. When the apostles in Jerusalem heard that Samaria had received the word of God, they sent Peter and John, who came down and prayed for the new believers that they might receive the Holy Spirit, and laid their hands on them, and they received Him—the same gift, the same seal, given to the Samaritans as to us at Pentecost, that none of us might ever boast as though the grace were ours by birthright and not theirs by gift. But when Simon saw that the Spirit was given through the laying on of the apostles' hands, he offered them money, saying, "Give me this power also, that anyone on whom I lay my hands may receive the Holy Spirit." Peter rebuked him sharply: "May your silver perish with you, because you thought you could obtain the gift of God with money! You have neither part nor lot in this matter, for your heart is not right before God. Repent of this wickedness." Here was the same lesson as Ananias's, in another key: the gift of God cannot be bought, nor bent to serve a man's own greatness. Salvation is grace from first to last, and the moment a man tries to purchase it or use it for himself, he shows he has not understood it at all. The thing was free precisely because it was beyond all price.

I have lived long enough to see this pattern repeat in every generation, and it never fails to astonish me: that the enemies of the gospel, in their fury to destroy it, only scatter its seed the wider. They drove us out of Jerusalem to silence us, and we went everywhere preaching the word. They have burned our writings, and the copies multiplied; they have killed our preachers, and the blood of the martyrs has drawn more to the faith than any sermon. It is as though the Lord has so ordered things that the harder the world strikes at His church, the farther it flings the gospel abroad. I do not say we should seek persecution, nor that it is anything but grievous to bear; only that I have ceased to despair when the storm breaks upon us, for I have seen, again and again, that the wind which scatters us is the wind that sows the world.

Then an angel of the Lord said to Philip, "Rise and go toward the south, to the road that goes down from Jerusalem to Gaza." This is a desert place. And he rose and went, and behold, there was an Ethiopian, a eunuch, a court official of the Candace, queen of the Ethiopians, who was in charge of all her treasure. He had come to Jerusalem to worship and was returning home, seated in his chariot, and he was reading aloud the prophet Isaiah. The Spirit said to Philip, "Go over and join this chariot." So Philip ran to him and heard him reading Isaiah the prophet, and asked, "Do you understand what you are reading?" And the man answered, "How can I, unless someone guides me?" and invited Philip to come up and sit with him.

Now the passage he was reading was this: "Like a sheep he was led to the slaughter, and like a lamb before its shearer is silent, so he opens not his mouth. In his humiliation justice was denied him. Who can describe his generation? For his life is taken away from the earth." The eunuch asked, "About whom does the prophet say this, about himself or about someone else?" Then Philip opened his mouth, and beginning with this very Scripture he told him the good news about Jesus. As they went along the road they came to some water, and the eunuch said, "See, here is water! What prevents me from being baptized?" And he commanded the chariot to stop, and they both went down into the water, and Philip baptized him. And when they came up out of the water, the Spirit carried Philip away, and the eunuch saw him no more, and went on his way rejoicing.

When the account of it reached me, I sat a long while in wonder. A man from the very ends of the earth, a foreigner and an outsider in more ways than one, returning from a Jerusalem that could offer him only the outer courts, sat reading the song of the suffering servant—the very prophecy I had watched fulfilled with my own eyes at Golgotha, the lamb led to the slaughter who opened not his mouth—and asked the one question that mattered: of whom does the prophet speak? And a believer set on that road by the Spirit told him it was Jesus, and before the dust of the desert had settled, the man was carried down into the water and up again into the family of God, and went on his way rejoicing toward Africa. The plan was running far ahead of any of us now. The Lamb who takes away the sin of the world was being preached from an ancient scroll to an African official in a chariot in the wilderness, and the joy of the Samaritan well and the joy of Pentecost was kindled in one more heart, in one more nation. I marveled that nothing was wasted—not the prophet's words written seven centuries before, not the eunuch's long and costly pilgrimage, not even the persecution that had driven Philip out of Jerusalem and set him, of all places, on that lonely southern road at the very hour the chariot passed.

What has always struck me most is the smallness of it, set beside its greatness. There was no crowd here, no thronging city, no thousands cut to the heart—only one man, in a chariot, on an empty desert road, and one believer sent to run alongside him. The Spirit who had filled a whole house at Pentecost now arranged the meeting of two men in the middle of nowhere, because one searching soul was reading a scroll he could not understand. I have learned from it that the God who saves the multitudes does not despise the one; that He will set a whole sequence of providences in motion—an angel, a road, a chariot, a scroll opened to just the right page—for the sake of a single seeking heart. The shepherd who left the ninety-nine to go after the one was at work on that desert road, and is at work still, wherever one lost soul is feeling its way toward Him.

But the wonder that undid me most in all those days was Saul. He was still breathing threats and murder against the disciples of the Lord, not content to have hounded us out of Jerusalem, and he went to the high priest and asked for letters to the synagogues at Damascus, so that if he found any belonging to the Way, men or women, he might bring them bound to Jerusalem. He was the worst of all our enemies, the one whose very name made the scattered believers tremble and lower their voices, the man who had stood approving while Stephen was stoned and kept the killers' coats. And it was him—him of all men under heaven—that the Lord chose.

As he went on his way and approached Damascus, about noon, suddenly a light from heaven shone around him, brighter than the noonday sun, and he fell to the ground and heard a voice saying, "Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?" And he said, "Who are you, Lord?" And the answer came: "I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting. Rise and enter the city, and you will be told what you are to do." I have turned that exchange over in my mind more times than I can count. The Lord did not say, "Why do you persecute my people," but "why do you persecute me"—as though every blow Saul struck against the least and lowliest believer fell upon the Master Himself, so closely had He bound us to His own body that to touch us was to touch Him. Saul rose from the ground, and when he opened his eyes he could see nothing, and they led him by the hand into Damascus, and for three days he was without sight and neither ate nor drank.

Then the Lord called a disciple in Damascus named Ananias and sent him to Saul. Ananias was afraid, for he had heard how much evil this man had done to the saints in Jerusalem; but the Lord said, "Go, for he is a chosen instrument of mine to carry my name before the Gentiles and kings and the children of Israel, for I will show him how much he must suffer for the sake of my name." So Ananias went, and entered the house, and laid his hands on him and said, "Brother Saul"—brother, to the man who had come to drag him to prison—"the Lord Jesus, who appeared to you on the road, has sent me that you may regain your sight and be filled with the Holy Spirit." And immediately something like scales fell from his eyes, and he regained his sight and rose and was baptized, and took food and was strengthened. And at once he began to proclaim Jesus in the synagogues, saying, "He is the Son of God," so that all who heard were amazed and said, "Is not this the man who made havoc in Jerusalem of those who called upon this name?"

When the report reached us, we could scarcely believe it, and some among us feared it was a trick, a wolf pretending to be a sheep to root out the flock. But it was true. The chief persecutor, the man who had held the coats at Stephen's stoning, was now preaching with his whole soul the very faith he had set out to destroy, and was soon fleeing for his own life, lowered in a basket through a window in the wall by the disciples he had come to hunt. If grace could lay hold of Saul, then there was no one anywhere beyond its reach, and no sinner whose record was too black and bloody to be washed white as snow. The Lord had said, long before, on the night He sat at table with tax collectors, that He came not to call the righteous but sinners; and here was the proof of it blazing brighter than the Damascus noon. He had reached down out of heaven and seized His fiercest enemy by the throat of his own hatred and made him His most ardent friend and His chosen instrument to the nations. I had thought, after the cross and the empty tomb, that I had finally measured the depth of His mercy. Saul taught me that I had not yet seen the bottom of it, and never would. And so the church throughout all Judea and Galilee and Samaria, no longer hunted by that man, had peace and was built up, and walking in the fear of the Lord and the comfort of the Holy Spirit, it multiplied.

I have pondered, too, the gentleness hidden inside the severity of that noon. The light struck Saul blind and threw him to the ground—but the voice did not destroy him, as it might justly have destroyed the man who was hauling the saints to prison and death. It asked him a question: "Why do you persecute me?" The Lord came to His enemy not with a thunderbolt but with a question, the question of a wounded love seeking to be understood. And He sent, to the blinded persecutor, not an avenging angel but a trembling disciple who called him "Brother Saul." I think the Lord meant from the very first not to crush Saul but to win him, to break him only so far as was needed to make him new. And I have taken great comfort from it, for I have learned that when the Lord lays a man low, it is most often not to destroy him but to save him, and that the same hand which strikes us blind is the hand that means to give us sight we never had before.

Peter, traveling here and there among all the churches in those days of peace, came down to the saints who lived at Lydda. There he found a man named Aeneas, bedridden for eight years and paralyzed. Peter said to him, "Aeneas, Jesus Christ heals you; rise and make your bed." And immediately he rose, and all who lived in Lydda and the plain of Sharon saw him and turned to the Lord. Near there, at Joppa by the sea, was a disciple named Tabitha, which means Dorcas, a woman full of good works and acts of charity, who had clothed the widows of the city with garments made by her own hands. In those days she fell sick and died, and they washed her body and laid it in an upper room and sent for Peter. When he came, the widows stood beside him weeping and showing the tunics and cloaks she had made while she was with them. Peter put them all outside, and knelt down and prayed, and then, turning to the body, said, "Tabitha, arise." And she opened her eyes, and seeing Peter she sat up. He gave her his hand and raised her up, and called the saints and widows and presented her alive.

I smiled when I heard it, and wept a little too, for it was the old pattern still at work, unchanged. "Tabitha, arise" was so near to "Talitha, cumi"—the very words I had heard the Lord speak by Jairus' bed, when He took a dead girl by the hand and warmed her cold fingers back to life—that I knew at once whose power was moving through Peter's outstretched hand. The Lord who had taken death by the hand in Galilee was taking it by the hand still, through His servants, and the weeping widows of Joppa knew the same joy as that mother long ago. Death was learning, town by town, that it no longer had the last word where the name of Jesus was spoken.

It moved me, when I heard of Tabitha, that the church remembered her not for any great work or office but for the tunics and cloaks she had sewn with her own hands for the poor widows of Joppa. They stood weeping and holding up the garments she had made. Hers was a hidden life of small mercies, the kind the world never records; and yet the Lord raised her by name, and her story is told now in every nation under heaven. I have learned from her that nothing done in love for the least of His people is ever truly small or ever truly lost. The Lord keeps a different account than the world keeps. The widow's two coins, the cup of cold water, the garments sewn for the poor—these are treasured up in heaven, while the monuments of the proud crumble; and on the last day it will be the Tabithas, and not the Herods, who are found to have built something that lasts.

Then the Lord set in motion a thing that would widen the church beyond anything we in Jerusalem had yet dared to imagine. In Caesarea there was a centurion named Cornelius, of the Italian Cohort, a devout man who feared God with all his household, who gave alms generously and prayed continually—and yet a Gentile, an uncircumcised Roman soldier, a man outside the covenant and the promises. One afternoon an angel of God came to him in a vision and told him his prayers and alms had come up as a memorial before God, and bade him send to Joppa for Peter. And the next day, as his men drew near the city, Peter went up on the roof of Simon the tanner's house to pray, about the sixth hour, and became hungry. While they prepared a meal he fell into a trance, and saw the heavens opened and something like a great sheet descending, let down by its four corners, full of all kinds of animals and reptiles and birds, clean and unclean together. And a voice said, "Rise, Peter; kill and eat." But Peter said, "By no means, Lord; for I have never eaten anything that is common or unclean." And the voice came again: "What God has made clean, do not call common." This happened three times, and then the sheet was taken up to heaven. While Peter puzzled over what it could mean, the men from Cornelius arrived at the gate, and the Spirit told him to go with them without hesitation, making no distinction.

So Peter went, taking some of the brothers from Joppa, and entering the house of a Gentile—a thing no observant Jew would lightly do—he found many gathered, and said, "You yourselves know how unlawful it is for a Jew to associate with or visit anyone of another nation, but God has shown me that I should not call any person common or unclean." And as he preached to them—how God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and power, how He went about doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil, how they put Him to death by hanging Him on a tree, and how God raised Him on the third day and made Him to appear, and how everyone who believes in Him receives forgiveness of sins through His name—while Peter was still speaking these words, the Holy Spirit fell on all who heard. The believers from among the circumcised who had come with Peter were amazed, because the gift of the Holy Spirit was poured out even on the Gentiles, for they heard them speaking in tongues and extolling God, just as we had at Pentecost. Then Peter said, "Can anyone withhold water for baptizing these people, who have received the Holy Spirit just as we have?" And he commanded them to be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ.

When the account of this reached me, the words of the Lord at the Samaritan well came rushing back, and the title the townsfolk had given Him there—the Savior of the world. I had believed it, and yet I confess that some narrow, stubborn corner of my heart had still half expected the Gentiles to come in, when they came, by some lesser door, as guests admitted to the edge of the feast rather than as children seated at the table. But God had given them the very same Spirit, in the very same way, with the very same signs, with no thought of partiality at all. Peter said it best, standing in that Roman house: "Truly I understand that God shows no partiality, but in every nation anyone who fears Him and does what is right is acceptable to Him." The cross had torn the veil of the Temple from top to bottom; now it was tearing down the ancient wall between Jew and Gentile as well, the dividing wall of hostility that had stood as long as anyone could remember. And I saw, more clearly than ever before, that the family the Lord had prayed for in the upper room on the night He was betrayed—that they may all be one, as He and the Father are one—was to be gathered out of every nation under heaven, all of them coming in by the one and only door, which is Christ, and none of them by any worthiness of their own.

I have marveled, too, at the patience the Lord showed with Peter's slowness, and through Peter with all of us. It took a vision repeated three times, and the Spirit's plain command, and the men already knocking at the gate, to move Peter to go to a Gentile's house—so deep ran the old walls in even the best of us. We do not lay down our prejudices easily, even when grace has laid hold of us; the heart clings to its old distinctions and its old contempts long after the gospel has, in truth, abolished them. But the Lord was gentle and persistent with Peter, leading him step by step until he could say with his own mouth that God shows no partiality. And I have taken comfort from it, for I too have had to be led, slowly and against my own resistance, into the full breadth of His mercy; and He has never grown weary of leading me, nor cast me off for being slow to learn how wide His love truly is.

When Peter returned to Jerusalem, those of the circumcision party criticized him, saying, "You went to uncircumcised men and ate with them." But Peter told them the whole story in order—the sheet, the voice, the men at the gate, the Spirit falling on the Gentiles exactly as on us at the beginning—and he ended, "If then God gave the same gift to them as He gave to us when we believed in the Lord Jesus Christ, who was I that I could stand in God's way?" And when they heard these things, they fell silent, and then they glorified God, saying, "Then to the Gentiles also God has granted repentance that leads to life." I have treasured that little phrase ever since—that God granted repentance—for it reminded me again of a truth I am always in danger of forgetting: that even our turning to Him is His gift and not our achievement. He does not stand at a distance waiting for us to manufacture a change of heart and present it to Him as our contribution; He works the change Himself, opening blind eyes and softening hard hearts, in Jew and Gentile alike. The whole of it, from first to last, is grace.

Meanwhile those who had been scattered by the persecution that arose over Stephen traveled as far as Phoenicia and Cyprus and Antioch, speaking the word at first to Jews only. But some of them, men of Cyprus and Cyrene, came to Antioch and began speaking to the Greeks also, preaching the Lord Jesus, and the hand of the Lord was with them, and a great number who believed turned to the Lord. When the report reached the church in Jerusalem, they sent Barnabas to Antioch, and when he came and saw the grace of God, he was glad, and he exhorted them all to remain faithful to the Lord with steadfast purpose, for he was a good man, full of the Holy Spirit and of faith. Then Barnabas went off to Tarsus to look for Saul, and when he had found him he brought him to Antioch, and for a whole year they met with the church and taught a great many people. And it was in Antioch that the disciples were first called Christians—Christ's ones, the people of the Anointed.

I liked that name from the first time I heard it, and I like it still. It put Him at the center, where He belongs, for we were not known by a teaching we held or a rule we kept or a place we worshiped, but by a Person—the One whose name was the only name under heaven by which we are saved, the name into which we were baptized, the name we suffered for and would, many of us, die for. To be a Christian was simply to belong to Christ. And about that time some prophets came down from Jerusalem, and one named Agabus foretold by the Spirit a great famine over all the world, which came to pass in the days of Claudius. So the disciples, each according to his ability, determined to send relief to the brothers living in Judea, and they did so, sending it by the hand of Barnabas and Saul. I noted with quiet joy that the grace lavished on the Gentiles in Antioch was already flowing back as practical love toward the poor Jewish believers in Jerusalem—the two halves of the new family, once divided by a wall of hostility, now sending bread to one another across the miles. The wall was truly down.

I have always thought it fitting that the name was first given to us at Antioch, and not at Jerusalem—that we were first called Christians not in the holy city of our fathers, with its Temple and its law, but in a great pagan crossroads of the Gentile world, where the gospel had broken out among the Greeks. For the name marked the new thing God was doing: gathering a people for Himself not out of one nation by birth but out of every nation by grace, a people defined no longer by descent from Abraham or by the marks of the law, but by belonging to Christ. And it was at Antioch, too, that this new people first sent relief back to the poor of Jerusalem—Gentile believers caring for Jewish believers across every old barrier of race and suspicion. The name and the love went together, and both said the same thing: the wall was down, and we were one in Him.

About that time—it would have been some fourteen years after the Lord's ascension—Herod the king laid violent hands on some who belonged to the church. He killed James the brother of John with the sword. The news struck me like a physical blow, and I grieve him to this day. James, one of the three the Lord had taken up the high mountain to see His glory; one of the sons of thunder who had once wanted to call down fire on a Samaritan village and had asked, with his brother, to sit at the Lord's right hand and left in His kingdom—now the first of the apostles to drink the cup. And I remembered the Lord's own words to the two brothers that day, when they asked for the thrones: that they did not know what they were asking, but that they would indeed drink the cup that He drank. James had been granted the very thing he once so boldly requested—a place near his Lord—though not at all in the way he had imagined it, for the road to that place ran through a martyr's death by Herod's sword. He had asked for glory and been given the cross first, as his Master had been; and I do not doubt that he understood, at the end, and was content.

When Herod saw that it pleased the Jews, he proceeded to arrest Peter also, during the days of Unleavened Bread, and put him in prison, delivering him to four squads of soldiers to guard him, intending after the Passover to bring him out to the people. So Peter was kept in prison, but earnest prayer for him was made to God by the church. And on the very night before Herod was to bring him out, while Peter slept between two soldiers, bound with two chains, and sentries stood at the door, an angel of the Lord stood beside him and a light shone in the cell, and the chains fell off his hands, and the angel led him past the guards and through the iron gate leading into the city, which opened of its own accord. When Peter came to himself, he went to the house of Mary, the mother of John Mark, where many were gathered together praying for him. He knocked at the door of the gateway, and a servant girl named Rhoda came to answer, and recognizing Peter's voice, in her joy she did not open the gate but ran in and told them that Peter was standing there, and they said to her, "You are out of your mind." I have laughed often at that small and very human detail across the years—that we were gathered praying earnestly for Peter's release, and could not believe it when the answer came knocking at the door. We pray, and still we are astonished when God answers.

Not long after, Herod went down to Caesarea, and when the people of Tyre and Sidon flattered him as a god, crying out that his voice was the voice of a god and not of a man, he accepted their worship and gave God no glory, and immediately an angel of the Lord struck him down, and he was eaten by worms and died. But the word of God increased and multiplied. The contrast was not lost on me, and I have never forgotten it: the king who grasped at glory and let men worship him rotted away in a single dreadful day, while the gospel he had tried to silence by the sword only grew the faster. So it always is. The proud man who exalts himself is brought low, and the humble word he despised goes on conquering the world.

I have set the two deaths of that chapter side by side many times in my mind—James, struck down by the sword of an earthly king, and Herod, struck down by the angel of the King of heaven. To the eye of the world, James was the loser: a leader of the church cut off early, while the tyrant flourished and was praised as a god. But the world's eye sees only the surface of things. James went home to his Lord, to the place near the throne that he had asked for long ago; Herod was carried off by worms in his pride and was no more. I have lived long enough to watch this pattern repeat in many lives, and I no longer envy the Herods their season of glory, nor pity the James their seeming defeat. The Lord's servants may fall to the sword, but they fall upward, into His arms; it is the proud who exalt themselves against Him who truly fall, and there is no rising from that fall.

In the church at Antioch there were prophets and teachers—Barnabas, and Simeon who was called Niger, and Lucius of Cyrene, and Manaen who had been brought up with Herod the tetrarch, and Saul. While they were worshiping the Lord and fasting, the Holy Spirit said, "Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them." So after fasting and praying, they laid their hands on them and sent them off—and thus, in a quiet room of praying men, began the journeys that would carry the gospel across the world. I have thought it fitting that it started not with a strategy of men but with the Spirit's own word, and not with the famous apostles in Jerusalem but with a mixed company in Antioch, a Cyprian Levite and a converted persecutor and men of Africa and a foster-brother of a king. The Lord chooses His instruments where He will, and sends them out by His own breath.

Being sent by the Holy Spirit, they went down to Seleucia and sailed to Cyprus, Barnabas's home country, and proclaimed the word of God in the synagogues, with John Mark to assist them. When they had gone through the whole island as far as Paphos, they came upon a magician, a Jewish false prophet named Bar-Jesus, who was with the proconsul Sergius Paulus, a man of intelligence who summoned Barnabas and Saul, wishing to hear the word of God. But the magician opposed them, seeking to turn the proconsul away from the faith. Then Saul, who is also called Paul—and from this point I came to know him by that name—filled with the Holy Spirit, looked intently at him and said, "You son of the devil, you enemy of all righteousness, full of all deceit and villainy, will you not stop making crooked the straight paths of the Lord? And now, behold, the hand of the Lord is upon you, and you will be blind." And immediately mist and darkness fell upon him, and he went about seeking someone to lead him by the hand. Then the proconsul believed, astonished at the teaching of the Lord. I marked the strange justice in it: the man who had tried to keep another in spiritual darkness was himself struck blind for a season, as Saul himself once had been on the Damascus road—and I wondered whether Paul, leading words of judgment against a blinded man, remembered the hand that had once led him, blinded, into the city, and the grace that had given him back his sight. Even his severity was the severity of one who had been shown mercy.

It has not escaped me that the great mission to the nations began in a meeting for worship and fasting, with no plan of men at all, only the Spirit's word: "Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul." We did not devise the strategy that carried the gospel across the world; the Spirit did, and He sent out whom He chose, when He chose. I have watched men since try to spread the faith by their own cleverness and their own schemes, and accomplish little; and I have watched the Lord take unlikely men, set apart by His Spirit in some obscure gathering of prayer, and through them shake the nations. The work is His, the sending is His, the increase is His. Our part is to worship and to wait and to obey when He speaks, and to go where He sends, trusting that the One who calls is the One who will accomplish through us far more than we could ever have planned.

From Paphos Paul and his companions set sail and came to Perga in Pamphylia, where John Mark left them and returned to Jerusalem—a parting that would later cause grief between Paul and Barnabas. They went on to Antioch in Pisidia, and on the Sabbath they entered the synagogue and sat down, and after the reading of the Law and the Prophets the rulers sent word inviting them to speak any word of encouragement they had. So Paul stood up, motioned with his hand, and preached a sermon that, when it was later repeated to us, I recognized at once as the very heart of all that we had learned at the Lord's own feet.

He told the story of Israel—the choosing of the fathers, the deliverance from Egypt, the wilderness, the judges, Samuel, Saul, and then David, a man after God's own heart. And from David's line, Paul said, God had brought to Israel a Savior, Jesus, as He had promised, of whom John the Baptist had gone before preaching. The people of Jerusalem and their rulers, not recognizing Him nor understanding the very prophets they read every Sabbath, had condemned Him and asked Pilate to have Him executed, and when they had carried out all that was written of Him, they took Him down from the tree and laid Him in a tomb. But God raised Him from the dead, and He appeared for many days to those who had come up with Him from Galilee—and I caught my breath when this was repeated to me, for he meant us, the witnesses, the very company I belonged to. Then Paul came to the point of it all, and ended with words I have never been able to forget: "Let it be known to you therefore, brothers, that through this man forgiveness of sins is proclaimed to you, and by him everyone who believes is freed from everything from which you could not be freed by the law of Moses."

Freed from everything that the law could never free us from. I had sat under that law my whole life; I knew its weight in my bones, the way it named every debt and forgave none, the way it could show me my sickness in perfect detail and never once heal it. And here was the whole gospel pressed into a single sentence: what the law could only condemn, Christ had paid; the debts we could never be acquitted of by our own keeping, we were freely acquitted of by simply believing in Him. The next Sabbath nearly the whole city gathered to hear the word of the Lord, and when the jealous leaders contradicted Paul and reviled him, he and Barnabas turned boldly and said, "It was necessary that the word of God be spoken first to you. Since you thrust it aside and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we are turning to the Gentiles." And the Gentiles rejoiced and glorified the word of the Lord, and as many as were appointed to eternal life believed, and the word spread throughout the whole region. The seed the Lord had once sown in His parables, that had seemed to fall on so many hard and thorny hearts, was now bearing its hundredfold harvest among peoples we had been raised to think outside the very reach of God's mercy.

When this sermon was repeated to me, I noticed that Paul preached the same gospel to the synagogue at Pisidian Antioch that Peter had preached at Pentecost and that the Lord Himself had opened to us from Moses and the Prophets: that the Christ must suffer and rise, and that through Him forgiveness of sins is offered freely to all who believe. It was always the same gospel, in every mouth and every city—not Peter's gospel or Paul's gospel or John's, but the one gospel of the grace of God in the crucified and risen Christ. I have learned to be wary of any teacher who brings some new and different message, some deeper secret beyond this; for there is no gospel beyond the cross and the empty tomb, and the moment a man begins to preach himself, or some novelty of his own, he has left the only road that leads home. The treasure was never new or clever; it was always Christ, and Him crucified, and risen, and offered to sinners.

At Iconium they went together into the Jewish synagogue and spoke in such a way that a great number of both Jews and Greeks believed, and they remained a long time, speaking boldly for the Lord, who bore witness to the word of His grace by granting signs and wonders to be done by their hands. But the city was divided, as it always was where Christ was truly preached, some siding with the Jews and some with the apostles, until an attempt was made to stone them and they fled to Lystra and Derbe.

At Lystra there sat a man crippled in his feet from birth, who had never walked. He listened as Paul spoke, and Paul, looking at him and seeing that he had faith to be made well, said in a loud voice, "Stand upright on your feet." And the man sprang up and began to walk. But the crowds, when they saw it, lifted up their voices in the Lycaonian tongue, crying that the gods had come down to them in the likeness of men, and they called Barnabas Zeus and Paul Hermes, and the priest of Zeus brought oxen and garlands, meaning to offer sacrifice to them. When the apostles heard of it they tore their garments and rushed into the crowd, crying, "Men, why are you doing these things? We also are men, of like nature with you, and we bring you good news, that you should turn from these vain things to a living God." Even so they scarcely restrained the people from sacrificing to them. And then, in the sudden and terrible turning that crowds are so capable of, Jews came from Antioch and Iconium and won the people over, and they stoned Paul and dragged him out of the city, supposing him dead. But the disciples gathered about him, and he rose up and went on—the very man who had once held the coats of those who stoned Stephen now left for dead under a hail of stones for the name he had once tried to destroy.

On their way back they passed again through Lystra and Iconium and Antioch, strengthening the souls of the disciples and encouraging them to continue in the faith, telling them, "Through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God." And they appointed elders in every church, and with prayer and fasting committed them to the Lord in whom they had believed. Then they sailed back to Antioch, where they had first been commended to the grace of God for the work they had now fulfilled, and they gathered the church together and declared all that God had done with them, and how He had opened a door of faith to the Gentiles. I drank in every word of their report when it reached us. The Shepherd who had once gone after a single lost sheep in the hills of Galilee was now gathering whole flocks out of the nations—and He was doing it through a man who had once hunted His sheep to the death, so that every city Paul entered was itself a standing proof that the Lord came to seek and to save the lost, and that no sinner is beyond the reach of the grace that had seized him.

That word Paul and Barnabas spoke to the young disciples on their return has stayed with me through all my own afflictions: "Through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God." They did not promise the new believers an easy road; they had themselves just been stoned and left for dead, and they hid nothing of the cost. I have seen much harm done by those who promise that the followers of Christ will be spared trouble and given ease and prosperity in this life, for when the trouble comes, as it surely does, such believers are shaken and fall away, thinking God has failed them. But the Lord Himself told us plainly that in the world we would have tribulation, and that whoever would come after Him must take up his cross. The crown is real, and it is coming; but the road to it runs through the tribulation, as the road to the Lord's own crown ran through Gethsemane and Golgotha. The servant is not greater than his Master.
§§ The Letter of James

It was in these years, I believe, before the great question of the Gentiles was settled, that the first of the letters began to pass from hand to hand among us—the letter of James, the Lord's own brother, who had become a pillar of the church in Jerusalem. I knew James well. I had watched him grow from one of the brothers who did not believe, who once thought the Lord beside Himself, into a man so given to prayer that those who knew him said his knees had grown calloused like a camel's from the hours he spent on them in the Temple. His letter was plain and pointed and unadorned, full of the salt and savor of his brother's own teaching, and to read it was like hearing the Sermon on the Mount again in a new and homely voice.
