He wrote of counting it all joy when we meet trials of various kinds, knowing that the testing of our faith produces steadfastness, and that the steadfast man will receive the crown of life. He wrote that every good and perfect gift comes down from the Father of lights, with whom there is no shadow of turning, and that of His own will He brought us forth by the word of truth—our new birth, like everything else, His doing and not ours. He charged us to be doers of the word and not hearers only, deceiving ourselves; to be quick to hear and slow to speak and slow to anger; to bridle the tongue, that small fire that can set a whole forest ablaze; to seek the wisdom from above, which is pure, peaceable, gentle, full of mercy and good fruits. He wrote hard, scorching words to the rich who hoarded their wealth and defrauded the laborers in their fields, and tender words about visiting orphans and widows in their affliction, which he called religion pure and undefiled before God. And he insisted, in words that some have thought stood at odds with Paul, that faith without works is dead—that a faith which sees a brother naked and hungry and says only "Go in peace, be warmed and filled" without giving him what he needs cannot save anyone, for it is no more alive than a body without a spirit.

I never heard James and Paul as enemies, though, however much some have tried to set them against each other. Paul told us how a sinner is first set right before God—by faith alone, apart from any works of the law, lest any man should boast. James told us what a living faith looks like once it has been planted in a heart—that it cannot help but put out the fruit of mercy and good works, as surely as a healthy tree cannot help but bear. The one was speaking of the root, the other of the fruit, and both were pointing to the very same tree, planted by the very same grace. For a faith that had truly received the mercy I had watched poured out from the cross could no more sit idle while a brother starved than that forgiven servant in the Lord's parable could rightly seize his fellow by the throat over a hundred denarii. The mercy we received was never meant to be hoarded; it was meant to flow, and a faith through which it does not flow is no faith at all, but a dead and empty profession.

I have heard men set James against Paul as though they were two teachers at war, but I knew them both, and I tell you they were of one mind, like two watchmen guarding the same treasure from thieves who came at it from opposite sides. Paul guarded the gospel from those who would add their works to the finished work of Christ, and so he thundered that we are justified by faith alone, apart from works. James guarded that same gospel from those who would claim a faith that changed nothing, that left the heart cold and the hands closed and the brother still hungry; and so he insisted that a faith which produces no works is dead, no faith at all. The one said: you cannot be saved by your works. The other said: but the faith that saves you will not leave you without works. Both were defending the very same grace—the grace that justifies the ungodly freely, and then so changes them that they cannot help but love.
§§ Galatians

Not long after, another letter came, this one from Paul to the churches of Galatia that he had founded on that first journey, and it carried an urgency, even a holy heat, that startled me when I first heard it read aloud. For certain men had come among those young Gentile believers after Paul had gone, insisting that to be truly saved they must be circumcised and keep the law of Moses—that Christ alone was not enough, that grace needed the law's help to finish the work it had begun. Paul was astonished that they were so quickly deserting the One who had called them in grace and turning to a different gospel, which was no gospel at all; and he wrote that if anyone, even an angel from heaven, should preach a gospel contrary to the one they had received, let him be accursed.

He set the truth down more sharply than I had ever heard it put. "We know," he wrote, "that a person is not justified by works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ, so we also have believed in Christ Jesus, in order to be justified by faith in Christ and not by works of the law, because by works of the law no one will be justified." And he pressed it to its sharpest edge: "If righteousness were through the law, then Christ died for no purpose." He told the story of his own conversion, the persecutor seized by grace on the Damascus road, and how he had not received his gospel from men but from the Lord Himself; and how he had withstood even Peter to his face at Antioch when Peter, fearing the circumcision party, had drawn back from eating with the Gentile believers, for the very truth of the gospel was at stake in that table—whether we are accepted by God on the ground of our pedigree and our performance, or on the ground of Christ alone. And he wrote the words that I have carried as my own confession ever since, that I have whispered to myself in the dark and that I should like to die saying: "I have been crucified with Christ. It is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me. And the life I now live in the flesh I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave Himself for me."

I read that and wept, for it gathered up everything—the cup He sweated over in the garden, the cross where He bore my forsakenness and cried out into the darkness, the stone rolled away, the breakfast on the beach, the Spirit poured into my heart at Pentecost—into one short sentence that a man could die clinging to. The law, Paul said, had been our guardian, like a stern tutor set over a child, until Christ came; but now that faith had come we were no longer under a guardian, for we were all sons of God through faith, and if sons, then heirs—and an heir does not earn his inheritance by his labor, he receives it because of who his father is. To add anything at all to the finished work of the cross, even the smallest work of our own, was not to improve the gospel but to insult it, to say that the blood of the Son had not been quite enough. Christ had set us free for freedom; and Paul, who had once been the most zealous slave of the law alive, would not stand by and watch anyone slip back into the yoke of trying to save himself, when the saving had already been done.

I have noticed how fiercely Paul wrote in this letter, with none of his usual thanksgiving at the start, only astonishment and warning; and I have come to understand why. It was because the very gospel was at stake. There is a kind of error that is only a stumble, and the Lord is patient with it; but there is a kind that strikes at the root, that adds something of our own to the cross and so empties the cross of its power, and against that Paul would not yield for a moment, no, not even to an angel from heaven. For if we must finish by our own works what Christ began by His grace, then we are thrown back upon ourselves, and the good news is no news at all, only the old despair of trying to save ourselves. I have learned from Paul's holy anger to hold this one thing above all others: that salvation is by grace, through faith, in Christ alone, plus nothing; and that to add to it is not to enrich it but to destroy it.

The dispute that Paul's letter to the Galatians had answered came at last to a head in Jerusalem, and I was there for it. Men had come down from Judea to Antioch and were teaching the brothers, "Unless you are circumcised according to the custom of Moses, you cannot be saved." Paul and Barnabas had no small disagreement and debate with them, and so the church appointed that they, with some others, should go up to Jerusalem to the apostles and elders about this question. I count that gathering one of the most important I ever witnessed, for the gospel itself was on the scales, and whichever way the council leaned would shape the faith for every generation after us.

There was much debate. Then Peter rose and reminded the assembly how in the early days God had chosen that the Gentiles should hear the word of the gospel through his mouth, in the house of Cornelius, and how God, who knows the heart, had borne witness to them by giving them the Holy Spirit just as He had to us, and had made no distinction between us and them, having cleansed their hearts by faith. "Now, therefore," Peter said, "why are you putting God to the test by placing a yoke on the neck of the disciples that neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear? But we believe that we will be saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, just as they will." The whole assembly fell silent and listened as Barnabas and Paul related the signs and wonders God had done through them among the Gentiles. And then James—the Lord's brother, whom all of us honored—gave the judgment, citing the prophets who had foretold that the Gentiles would seek the Lord: that we should not trouble those of the Gentiles who turned to God, but write to them only to abstain from a few things that would needlessly wound their Jewish brothers, so that the two might live as one family at one table.

I have pondered Peter's words ever since, for there is a whole world in them. He did not say the Gentiles would be saved in the same way we Jews were; he said the very opposite—that we will be saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, just as they will. We Jews, with all our law and our covenants and our circumcision and our long inheritance of promises, would be saved by the very same grace, through the very same faith, as the uncircumcised pagans of Antioch and Caesarea. The council might have hung the heavy yoke of the law upon the necks of the Gentiles; instead it confessed before God that there is only one way of salvation for any soul that has ever lived, and that way is grace alone. It was the truth of the parable of the two sons spoken aloud in a council chamber: both sons, the law-keeping elder brother and the wandering younger one, come into the father's feast only by the father's mercy, and neither of them earns his place at the table. The church sent a letter of freedom back to Antioch, and when it was read aloud to the gathered believers, they rejoiced at the encouragement, for the gospel of grace had been guarded, and the door to the nations had been held open.

I have thought since that the whole future of the church hung on the judgment of that council, more than any of us fully knew at the time. Had they decided that the Gentiles must take up the law of Moses to be saved, the gospel of free grace would have been buried under the old yoke, and the good news would have become merely a new and heavier set of rules. But the Spirit guided them to confess the one thing that matters: that there is one way of salvation for all, Jew and Gentile alike, and that way is grace through faith. I have watched the church, in the generations since, tempted again and again to add some new requirement, some mark or work or rule by which men must earn their standing; and every time, the council at Jerusalem stands as a witness against it. The yoke we could not bear has been carried for us. We are saved, every one of us, the same way—by the grace of the Lord Jesus.

After some days Paul said to Barnabas, "Let us return and visit the brothers in every city where we proclaimed the word of the Lord, and see how they are." Barnabas wanted to take John Mark along, but Paul thought it best not to take one who had deserted them in Pamphylia and had not gone with them to the work. The disagreement between them grew so sharp that they parted ways; Barnabas took Mark and sailed to Cyprus, while Paul chose Silas and went through Syria and Cilicia, strengthening the churches. It grieved me to hear of the rift between two such men, who had labored and suffered side by side; yet I have lived long enough to see the Lord weave even our quarrels into His purposes, for now there were two missions where there had been one, and Mark, restored in time, became useful again and gave us, they say, the first written account of the Lord's life. The Lord does not need us to be flawless to use us; He works through cracked and quarreling vessels, as He always has.

At Lystra Paul found a disciple named Timothy, the son of a believing Jewish woman and a Greek father, well spoken of by the brothers, and he took him along, and so the second journey gathered its company. They went through the region of Phrygia and Galatia, having been kept by the Holy Spirit from speaking the word in Asia, and when they attempted to go into Bithynia, the Spirit of Jesus did not allow them. So they passed by Mysia and came down to Troas, on the very edge of the continent, and there in the night Paul saw a vision: a man of Macedonia standing and pleading with him, "Come over to Macedonia and help us." And immediately we sought to go on into Macedonia, concluding that God had called us to preach the gospel to them. So the good news that had begun in a small Galilean village, by a lake among fishermen, crossed the sea into Europe, carried by a handful of men who went where the Spirit drove them, not where they had planned.

Setting sail from Troas, they came to Philippi, a leading city of that district of Macedonia and a Roman colony. On the Sabbath they went outside the gate to the riverside, where they supposed there was a place of prayer, and sat down and spoke to the women who had gathered there. One of them, named Lydia, a seller of purple goods from the city of Thyatira, a worshiper of God, listened, and the Lord opened her heart to pay attention to what was said by Paul. She was baptized, and her household with her, and she prevailed upon them to come and stay at her house. I have always loved that small phrase—the Lord opened her heart—for it tells the secret of every conversion I have ever witnessed, including my own. Paul spoke the words, but it was the Lord who opened the heart to receive them, as He had once opened my eyes by the Jordan when I thought I was finding Him. The first believer on that whole continent of Europe was a woman won not by clever argument but by the quiet sovereign work of God upon her heart.

There too a slave girl with a spirit of divination, who brought her owners much gain by fortune-telling, followed Paul and us, crying out, "These men are servants of the Most High God, who proclaim to you the way of salvation." When Paul, greatly annoyed, turned and commanded the spirit to come out of her in the name of Jesus Christ, it came out that very hour. But when her owners saw that their hope of gain was gone, they seized Paul and Silas and dragged them before the magistrates, and the crowd joined in attacking them, and the magistrates had them beaten with rods and thrown into prison, their feet fastened in the stocks. About midnight, however, as Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God, and the other prisoners were listening, suddenly there was a great earthquake, so that the foundations of the prison were shaken, and immediately all the doors were opened and everyone's bonds were unfastened. The jailer, waking and seeing the prison doors open, drew his sword and was about to kill himself, supposing the prisoners had escaped. But Paul cried with a loud voice, "Do not harm yourself, for we are all here." And the jailer called for lights and rushed in, and trembling with fear he fell down before Paul and Silas and brought them out and asked the one question that finally matters above every other: "Sirs, what must I do to be saved?" And they said, "Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved, you and your household." That very night he washed their wounds and was baptized at once, he and all his family, and he set food before them and rejoiced that he had believed in God.

I have always loved that scene, for it holds the whole gospel pressed into a single night. A man with a sword already at his own throat, ready to die in despair, asks how he can be saved, and the answer is not a list of works to perform or a yoke of laws to take up, not years of penance or a lifetime of proving himself—but a Person to trust: believe in the Lord Jesus. The very same answer that had saved the dying thief who could do nothing but ask to be remembered, that had justified the tax collector who beat his breast and begged for mercy, that had caught Peter sinking beneath the waves when he cried, "Lord, save me." Believe, and be saved, you and your household. And the song that the two men had been singing with their backs torn and bleeding in the dark, before ever the earthquake came, told me that they had already found a freedom that no prison and no stocks could touch—the freedom of men who knew themselves saved, and could not stop singing about it even in chains.

I have set the two conversions of Philippi side by side many times—Lydia, the prosperous dealer in purple, whose heart the Lord opened quietly as she listened by the river, and the jailer, a rough man with blood on his hands, brought to his knees by an earthquake in the dead of night. The one came gently, the other violently; the one was a seeking worshiper of God, the other a despairing man with a sword at his own throat. And yet they were saved in precisely the same way, by the same Lord, through the same simple word: believe. There is no single road by which men come to Christ—some He draws softly over long years, some He seizes in a moment of crisis—but there is only one door they all come through, and that door is faith in the Lord Jesus. I have learned never to doubt a conversion because it did not look like my own; the Lord opens hearts as He pleases, but it is always He who opens them.

When they had passed through Amphipolis and Apollonia, they came to Thessalonica, where there was a synagogue, and for three Sabbaths Paul reasoned with them from the Scriptures, explaining and proving that it was necessary for the Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead—the very thing the Lord Himself had opened to us from Moses and all the Prophets after His resurrection—and saying, "This Jesus, whom I proclaim to you, is the Christ." Some of them were persuaded and joined Paul and Silas, as did a great many of the devout Greeks and not a few of the leading women. But the Jews, moved by jealousy, gathered a mob, set the city in an uproar, and attacked the house of Jason, where the missionaries had lodged, dragging some of the brothers before the city authorities and shouting, "These men who have turned the world upside down have come here also." The accusation was truer than the accusers knew. The brothers sent Paul and Silas away by night to Berea, where the people were more noble than those in Thessalonica, for they received the word with all eagerness, examining the Scriptures daily to see if these things were so. Many of them therefore believed. I have always admired the Bereans, who would not take even Paul's word for it without searching the Scriptures themselves—for the gospel does not fear examination; it was written in the Law and the Prophets long before it was preached in the synagogues, and the more closely a man searches, the more surely he finds the Lord on every page.

I have admired the Bereans above almost any in this whole account, for they did the thing that I have come to think the very mark of an honest soul: they would not take even Paul's word for it, eloquent and Spirit-filled as he was, but searched the Scriptures daily to see whether these things were so. The gospel does not ask to be believed blindly, nor does it fear examination; it was written in the Law and the Prophets centuries before it was preached in the synagogues, and the more closely a man searches them, the more surely he finds the Lord on every page. I have warned many against the teacher who bids you simply trust him and not look too closely; that is the way of the deceiver. The true word of God invites the lamp and the long study, and grows only brighter under it. Search, and you will find Him there, as the Bereans did, and your faith will rest not on a man's eloquence but on the word of God that cannot be broken.

Now while Paul was waiting for Silas and Timothy at Athens, his spirit was provoked within him as he saw that the city was full of idols. So he reasoned in the synagogue with the Jews, and in the marketplace every day with whoever happened to be there, until some of the Epicurean and Stoic philosophers brought him to the Areopagus, wanting to hear this new teaching. And Paul stood in the midst of the Areopagus, among the altars and the statues and the proud wisdom of the Greeks, and said, "Men of Athens, I perceive that in every way you are very religious. For as I passed along and observed the objects of your worship, I found also an altar with this inscription: To the unknown god. What therefore you worship as unknown, this I proclaim to you." He told them of the God who made the world and everything in it, who does not live in temples made by hands nor is served by human hands as though He needed anything, since He Himself gives to all mankind life and breath and everything; who made from one man every nation, that they should seek Him and perhaps feel their way toward Him and find Him, though He is not far from any one of us, for in Him we live and move and have our being. "The times of ignorance God overlooked," Paul said, "but now He commands all people everywhere to repent, because He has fixed a day on which He will judge the world in righteousness by a man whom He has appointed, and of this He has given assurance to all by raising Him from the dead." Now when they heard of the resurrection of the dead, some mocked, but others said, "We will hear you again about this." Some men joined him and believed, among them Dionysius the Areopagite and a woman named Damaris. I marveled, when the account reached me, at how Paul preached the same crucified and risen Christ to the philosophers of Athens as to the synagogues of Judea, neither flattering their wisdom nor borrowing it, but calling even the cleverest men in the world to do the one thing every soul must do—to repent and turn to the living God, and to reckon with the man God raised from the dead, before whom they would all one day stand.

I have admired how Paul stood among the philosophers of Athens and neither flattered their wisdom nor was cowed by it. He met them on their own ground, quoting their own poets, reasoning from the altar to their unknown god, and yet he bent not one inch on the things that mattered: that God commands all men everywhere to repent, and that He has appointed a day of judgment by the man He raised from the dead. He did not trim the gospel to please the clever, nor leave out the resurrection because he knew they would mock it—and mock it they did. I have learned from him that we are to be wise in how we speak to each kind of hearer, becoming all things to all men that we might win some, but that there is a core we must never surrender to be thought reasonable: the cross, the resurrection, the call to repent. The world will always laugh at a risen Christ; we must preach Him anyway, for some, like Dionysius and Damaris, will believe.
§§ 1 & 2 Thessalonians

From Corinth, soon after, Paul wrote back to the young church in Thessalonica that he had been forced to leave so quickly under cover of night—and these, so far as I have ever known, were the first of his letters to be set down. He wrote to comfort believers under heavy persecution, and to steady them in their grief, for some of their number had died, and the survivors feared that those who had fallen asleep had somehow missed the Lord's return and lost their share in the glory to come.

Paul would not have them grieve as the rest do, who have no hope. "For since we believe that Jesus died and rose again," he wrote, "even so, through Jesus, God will bring with Him those who have fallen asleep. For the Lord Himself will descend from heaven with a cry of command, with the voice of an archangel and with the sound of the trumpet of God. And the dead in Christ will rise first. Then we who are alive, who are left, will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air, and so we will always be with the Lord. Therefore encourage one another with these words." And in a second letter, written soon after, he steadied them again, for some, thinking the day of the Lord had already come, had grown idle and alarmed; and he reminded them that the Lord would indeed come, and would grant relief to the afflicted and repay those who troubled them, and bade them stand firm and hold to what they had been taught.

I read those letters as a man who had stood on the Mount of Olives and watched the cloud take Him out of my sight, and heard the two men in white promise that He would come again in the same way as we had seen Him go. The hope that Paul held out to the Thessalonians was the very hope I had carried down that hill and carried still: that the salvation begun at the cross and sealed at the empty tomb was not yet complete, that the Shepherd who had died for the sheep and risen and poured out His Spirit would come once more in glory to gather His own and to right every wrong, and that not even death could rob a single believer of that day. The grave had given Lazarus back at His word; the grave had given the Lord Himself back on the third morning; and the grave would surely give back all who slept in Him. So we did not grieve as the others did. We buried our dead in hope, and laid them down as men lay down seed, and we encouraged one another with these words, and we lifted our eyes and watched the sky.

I have drawn more comfort from these letters in my old age than I can easily say, for I have buried many whom I loved, and I have felt the ache of the question the Thessalonians felt: what of those who fall asleep before He comes? Paul's answer is the answer I rest in as my own end draws near. We do not grieve as those who have no hope. The Lord who died and rose will bring with Him those who have fallen asleep in Him, and the dead in Christ will rise. I have stood at many gravesides now, and laid in the earth faces I shall not see again in this life, and I have learned to lay them down as a farmer lays down seed in the autumn ground—not throwing them away, but planting them, in the sure hope of a spring that is coming. The grave is not a wall but a door. I have watched the sky for Him since the day He ascended, and I watch it still, the more eagerly now that so many I love are waiting on the other side.

After Athens, Paul went to Corinth, a great and restless port city, rich and crowded and sunk deep in its idols and its pleasures, where two seas met and the sailors of the world passed through. There he found a Jewish tentmaker named Aquila, lately come from Italy with his wife Priscilla, because Claudius had ordered all the Jews to leave Rome; and because Paul was of the same trade, he stayed and worked with them, and reasoned in the synagogue every Sabbath, trying to persuade Jews and Greeks. When Silas and Timothy arrived from Macedonia, Paul was occupied with the word, testifying that the Christ was Jesus; and when the Jews opposed and reviled him, he shook out his garments and turned to the Gentiles.

And the Lord said to Paul one night in a vision, "Do not be afraid, but go on speaking and do not be silent, for I am with you, and no one will attack you to harm you, for I have many in this city who are my people." So he stayed a year and six months, teaching the word of God among them, and many of the Corinthians, hearing him, believed and were baptized—even Crispus, the ruler of the synagogue, with his entire household. I have held that word of the Lord close to my heart ever since I heard it, for it tells me how the gospel goes out into a city and takes root. "I have many in this city who are my people"—spoken before they had yet believed, while they were still pagans in a pagan city, worshiping idols and selling themselves in the temples. The Lord knew His sheep before ever the Shepherd's voice reached their ears; the harvest was already His and already counted before the first seed of preaching was sown. It was the same sovereign grace that had found me at the Jordan when I imagined I was finding Him, that had seen Nathanael under the fig tree before Philip ever called him, that had watched the prodigal's road for the first sign of a returning son. Paul preached, and men believed; and yet beneath all the preaching ran a deeper and quieter current—the Father giving His chosen people to the Son, calling to Himself those who were far off, so that no one who labors in the gospel can ever boast, for the increase is God's alone. When at last the Jews made a united attack on Paul and brought him before the proconsul Gallio, Gallio refused to judge a matter of their own law, and so Paul was left free to finish his work; and then, after some time, he sailed for Syria with Priscilla and Aquila, and came in time back to Antioch where it had all begun.

That word the Lord spoke to Paul in the night at Corinth—"I have many in this city who are my people"—has steadied me whenever the work seemed fruitless and the soil hard. For it told me that the harvest does not depend on the eloquence of the preacher or the openness of the city, but on the prior choice of God, who has His people even in the most corrupt of places, and will surely bring them in. Corinth was a byword for vice, a city given over to every idolatry and every appetite; and yet the Lord had many there who were His, and they came. I have learned not to write off any place or any person as beyond hope, for I do not know whom the Lord has chosen, and I have seen Him gather His own out of the unlikeliest of cities and the hardest of hearts. We sow and we water; but it is God who has the people, and God who gives the increase, and so we labor on in hope even where the ground looks barren.

After spending some time in Antioch, Paul set out again, passing through the region of Galatia and Phrygia in order, strengthening all the disciples—and so the third of his great journeys began. Now in those days there came to Ephesus a Jew named Apollos, a native of Alexandria, an eloquent man, mighty in the Scriptures. He had been instructed in the way of the Lord, and being fervent in spirit he spoke and taught accurately the things concerning Jesus, though he knew only the baptism of John. When Priscilla and Aquila heard him speaking boldly in the synagogue, they took him aside and explained to him the way of God more accurately, and he went on to be a great help to those who through grace had believed, powerfully refuting the Jews in public and showing by the Scriptures that the Christ was Jesus. I have always been moved that it was a tentmaker and his wife, two ordinary believers, who quietly took the brilliant Alexandrian aside and filled out what was lacking in his understanding—for the Lord builds His church not only through apostles and great preachers but through humble saints who know a little more of the truth and share it gently with those who know a little less.

While Apollos was at Corinth, Paul came to Ephesus and found there some disciples who had been baptized into John's baptism but had not so much as heard that there was a Holy Spirit. When Paul had explained the gospel more fully and baptized them in the name of the Lord Jesus, and laid his hands on them, the Holy Spirit came on them, and they spoke in tongues and prophesied—the same gift again, the same seal of the same salvation, given now to a handful of men on the far western edge of the world, just as it had been given at Pentecost in Jerusalem and at Caesarea in the house of Cornelius. I have noticed how the Spirit kept falling in this way, in city after city, on Jew and Samaritan and Gentile alike, always the same gift, as if God meant to leave no room for any people to imagine themselves first or favored. The salvation was one, the Spirit was one, the Lord was one, and all who came, came in the same way and received the same grace.

I have always been moved that it was Priscilla and Aquila, two ordinary tentmakers, who took the brilliant Apollos quietly aside and filled out what was lacking in his understanding. They did not shame him publicly, nor envy his gifts, nor stand off in fear of his learning; they simply, lovingly, in private, showed him the way of God more accurately, and so the church gained one of its greatest preachers. I have learned from them that the Lord builds His church not only through apostles and famous men but through humble saints who know a little more of the truth and share it gently with those who know a little less. Many a soul has been set right not by a sermon from a pulpit but by a quiet word from a faithful friend over a shared meal. We need not be eloquent to be useful; we need only to know the Lord, and to love our brother enough to lead him deeper in.

Paul entered the synagogue at Ephesus and spoke boldly for three months, and then, when some grew stubborn, he withdrew and reasoned daily in the hall of a man named Tyrannus, and this continued for two years, so that all the residents of Asia, both Jews and Greeks, heard the word of the Lord. And God did extraordinary miracles by the hands of Paul, so that even handkerchiefs and aprons that had touched his skin were carried to the sick, and their diseases left them and the evil spirits came out—the same power that I had once watched flow from the very hem of the Lord's garment in the streets of Galilee, flowing still through the cloth that touched His servant. Some itinerant Jewish exorcists, the seven sons of a man named Sceva, tried to use the name of Jesus as if it were a charm, commanding the spirits "by the Jesus whom Paul proclaims"; but the evil spirit answered, "Jesus I know, and Paul I recognize, but who are you?" and the man in whom the spirit was leaped on them and overpowered them, so that they fled out of the house naked and wounded. Fear fell on all the residents of Ephesus, and the name of the Lord Jesus was extolled. And many who had practiced magic arts brought their costly books together and burned them in the sight of all, and they counted the value of them and found it to be fifty thousand pieces of silver. A great fire of repentance, fifty thousand pieces of silver gone up in smoke and ash, because the men who had paid dearly for those dark arts now counted the freedom Christ gave them as worth more than all of it. I thought of the man freed of his legion in the country of the Gerasenes, and of these books burning in the streets of Ephesus, and I saw the same truth shining in both: that salvation is not only the forgiving of sin but the breaking of every chain, even the chains a man has spent his whole fortune to forge for himself. To be saved is to be set free.

So mightily did the word of the Lord grow and prevail that the silversmiths of Ephesus, who made silver shrines for the goddess Artemis and grew rich by them, began to fear for their trade. A man named Demetrius gathered the craftsmen and stirred them up, crying that this Paul was persuading people that gods made with hands are not gods at all, and that not only their trade but the temple of the great Artemis was in danger. The whole city was filled with confusion, and they rushed into the great theater shouting for some two hours, "Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!" until at last the town clerk quieted them and dismissed the assembly. It did not surprise me, when I heard of it, that the gospel had made enemies of the men who profited from the old darkness. The light always divides; I had seen it from the very beginning, on the Lord's own roads. Where Christ is truly preached, the idols lose their customers, the fortune-tellers lose their gain, and the men who sell darkness grow afraid—for the kingdom of God advances by setting captives free, and there is always someone who was making his living off the chains.

I have often thought of those costly books burning in the streets of Ephesus, fifty thousand pieces of silver curling into smoke and ash, and of what it must have cost those men to set them alight. They were not throwing away worthless things; they were burning a fortune, the very tools of their old trade and the source of their old power. But they had found something worth more, and they would not keep one foot in the old darkness while they walked in the new light. I have seen that this is what true repentance looks like—not merely a sorrow for sin, but a decisive turning away from it, a burning of the bridges back to the old life, however dear and costly those bridges may be. The Lord does not ask us to set down our chains reluctantly, keeping the key in our pocket; He gives us such a sight of His worth that we fling the chains gladly into the fire, counting all that we lose as rubbish compared to gaining Him.
§§ 1 Corinthians

From Ephesus, in those two years, Paul wrote to the church at Corinth, that beloved and deeply troubled flock he had labored a year and a half to gather, for reports had reached him of quarrels and pride and grave sins among them. His letter is long and searching and ranges over many things—divisions and lawsuits, marriage and food offered to idols, the gifts of the Spirit and the ordering of worship—but its foundation is laid in the opening pages, and that foundation has steadied me through many a storm. They were dividing into parties, boasting in their favorite teachers, one saying "I follow Paul," another "I follow Apollos," another "I follow Cephas," and puffing themselves up in their own wisdom and eloquence. Paul cut straight through all of it to the cross. "For the word of the cross is folly to those who are perishing," he wrote, "but to us who are being saved it is the power of God." He had not come to them, he reminded them, with lofty speech or wisdom, but had resolved to know nothing among them except Jesus Christ and Him crucified, lest the cross be emptied of its power by clever words.

I have turned that over many times—that the very thing the world counts foolish and weak, a Savior nailed to a Roman cross like a slave or a criminal, is in truth the wisdom and the power of God. The Greeks wanted clever arguments and the Jews demanded signs from heaven, but God was pleased to save the world through the folly of the cross, choosing what is low and despised in the world, even things that are not, to bring to nothing the things that are, so that no human being might boast in His presence. It was the lesson of the whole gospel set down as doctrine: that we are saved by what we could never have devised and never could deserve, so that all our boasting is emptied out and only one boast remains, that we boast in the Lord. Paul wrote to them of the Lord's Supper, repeating the very words I had heard with my own ears in the upper room—the bread that is His body, the cup of the new covenant in His blood—and warned them to discern that holy table rightly and not to profane it. He wrote that chapter on love that has been read at a thousand gatherings since, that though I speak with the tongues of men and of angels but have not love, I am only a noisy gong; that love is patient and kind, bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things, and never ends. And toward the close he laid down the foundation of our whole hope as plainly as it has ever been written: that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, that He was buried, that He was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures, and that He appeared to Cephas, then to the twelve, then to more than five hundred brothers at once, most of whom were still alive, and then to James, and last of all to Paul himself. I read his roll of witnesses and remembered, with a catch in my throat, that I was among that number—one of the company that had seen the risen Lord with our own eyes and touched Him with our own hands. And so I gave thanks that the hope on which I had staked my whole life was not a tale that we had spun out of our grief, but a thing that we had seen. For if Christ has not been raised, Paul wrote, our preaching is in vain and our faith is in vain, and we are still in our sins, and those who have fallen asleep have perished, and we are of all people most to be pitied. But in fact Christ has been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep; and as in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive; and the last enemy to be destroyed is death.

I have read this letter many times, and what strikes me most is that Paul answered a whole tangle of problems—divisions and pride and lawsuits and disorder at the Lord's table and confusion about the resurrection—by leading them back, again and again, to the cross. The Corinthians were enamored of wisdom and eloquence and spiritual showmanship, and Paul kept setting before them a crucified Savior, foolishness to the Greeks, a stumbling block to the Jews, but the wisdom and power of God to those being saved. I have come to see that nearly every sickness in a church can be traced to a forgetting of the cross, and nearly every cure is found in returning to it. Where men glory in their own wisdom or gifts or standing, the cross humbles them, for it says that we were saved by what we could never have devised and never could deserve. There is no boasting at the foot of the cross. And a people who truly remember how they were saved cannot long remain proud, or divided, or cold.
§§ 2 Corinthians

Paul's next letter to Corinth that reached us was the most tender and the most wounded of all his writings, poured out of a heart that had been through great affliction in Asia, where, as he said, he had been so utterly burdened beyond his strength that he despaired even of life itself, and had learned through it to rely not on himself but on God who raises the dead. He wrote of the comfort with which God comforts us in all our affliction, so that we may comfort others with the comfort we ourselves have received. He wrote of the surpassing treasure we carry in jars of clay—the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ, held in vessels as frail and breakable as our own mortal bodies, so that it might be plain to all that the surpassing power belongs to God and not to us. He wrote of being afflicted but not crushed, perplexed but not driven to despair, struck down but not destroyed; of an eternal weight of glory beyond all comparison being prepared for us through what he called our light and momentary affliction, while we look not to the things that are seen but to the things that are unseen.

But the words of his that have lodged the deepest in me, that I return to again and again, are those in which he laid bare the very mechanism of our rescue, the holy exchange at the heart of it all: "For our sake He made Him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God." I read that and I saw Golgotha again as if I stood beneath the cross once more. The One who knew no sin, the spotless Lamb, was made to be sin—my sin, and the sin of the world, laid upon His innocent and undeserving shoulders, until the forsakenness I had earned tore out of His lips in that cry into the darkness, My God, my God, why have you forsaken me. And in that same dread exchange, His righteousness was reckoned to me, so that I now stand before God clothed not in my own filthy rags but in the spotless robe of the Son. It is the greatest trade ever made in all the history of the world: He took what was mine, that I might receive what was His; He became what I was, that I might become what He is. Paul called this the ministry of reconciliation, and said that God was in Christ reconciling the world to Himself, not counting our trespasses against us, and that He had committed to us the message of this reconciliation, making us ambassadors for Christ, God making His appeal through us: "We implore you on behalf of Christ, be reconciled to God." And when Paul three times begged the Lord to take away a thorn in his flesh, a messenger of Satan sent to harass him, the answer he received has become my own comfort in every weakness and every grief: "My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness." So that even our frailty, our wounds, our thorns, become the very places where the grace of God is most clearly displayed, and we learn at last to boast not in our strength but in our weakness, that the power of Christ may rest upon us.

I have grown to love this wounded letter most of all Paul's writings, for in it he hides nothing of his weakness—his afflictions, his despair, his tears, the thorn that would not leave him, the burden that pressed him beyond his strength. And it is precisely there, in his weakness laid bare, that the grace of God shines brightest. "My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness." I have found this to be the very pattern of the Christian life, and never more than in my old age, as my strength fails and my body breaks down like the jar of clay it always was. The treasure was never in the vessel; it was always in the One who fills it. And so I have learned to glory not in what I can do but in what I cannot, that the power may plainly be His and not mine. The world seeks to be strong; the Lord teaches His people to be content in weakness, that they may lean wholly on Him, who raises the dead.
§§ Romans

It was from Corinth, in the few months before he turned his face toward Jerusalem with the collection for the poor, that Paul wrote the longest and weightiest of all his letters, sending it ahead to the believers in Rome whom he had never yet met, to prepare them for his coming and to set before them the gospel in full. When a copy of it at last reached us, I read it slowly, again and again, late into the nights, for it set out in good order the whole of the gospel I had lived—from the very depth of our ruin to the very height of our hope. I had walked the story on the roads of Galilee and Judea; Paul had written it down as doctrine, link by link, and the two fit together like a hand into a glove made for it.

He began with the bad news that alone makes the good news good: that the wrath of God is revealed against all ungodliness, that the Gentiles are without excuse for suppressing the truth and worshiping the creature rather than the Creator, and that the Jews, for all their law, are no better, for they break the very law in which they boast. All men, Jew and Greek alike, are under sin; none is righteous, no, not one; no one seeks for God; every mouth is stopped and the whole world is held accountable before Him; and by works of the law no human being will be justified in His sight, for through the law comes only the knowledge of sin. I knew the truth of every word of it in my own bones, for I had learned at the paralytic's torn-open roof in Capernaum that my deepest need was never my circumstances but my guilt, the sickness that no washing could reach. And then Paul turned the great corner into the heart of the matter, and I have never in all my life read words that gave me more joy than these: "But now the righteousness of God has been manifested apart from the law, although the Law and the Prophets bear witness to it—the righteousness of God through faith in Jesus Christ for all who believe. For there is no distinction: for all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God, and are justified by His grace as a gift, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus, whom God put forward as a propitiation by His blood, to be received by faith."

Justified by His grace as a gift. Not earned, not deserved, not paid for by anything in us, but given—the very thing I had watched happen with my own eyes a hundred times over: to the woman who wept on His feet and was told her sins were forgiven; to Zacchaeus, down out of his tree; to the thief at the last gasp, promised paradise that very day; to Saul, struck down on the Damascus road; and to me. Paul showed how Abraham himself was counted righteous not by working but by believing God, so that the promise might rest entirely on grace and be guaranteed to all his offspring. And he drew the blessed conclusion: that since we have been justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ—peace, where once there had been only enmity and that great fixed chasm I had heard the Lord describe. He set Adam beside Christ, the one man whose disobedience made the many sinners against the one man whose obedience makes the many righteous, the trespass against the free gift, and showed that where sin increased, grace abounded all the more.

I have read no letter more carefully than this one, nor returned to any more often, for in it Paul lays the whole foundation bare, stone by stone, and a man may build his soul upon it and not be moved. He begins where we least like to begin, with our ruin—that none is righteous, no, not one, that every mouth is stopped and the whole world stands guilty before God. I have known men who would not hear this, who thought themselves good enough, and they could find no joy in the gospel, for they did not know they needed it; the good news is only good to those who have first heard the bad. But once a man has truly seen that he is undone, that he cannot save himself, that the law can only condemn him—then the word "justified by His grace as a gift" falls on him like rain on cracked ground, and he understands at last why we call it good news. I had to be brought low at the paralytic's torn roof before I could be lifted up; and so must every soul that is saved.
§§ Romans (continued)

And then Paul rose, in the eighth chapter of that letter, to a height that I can still scarcely read aloud without trembling. "There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus." No condemnation—for the very ones who deserved nothing but condemnation, set free because the law of the Spirit of life had set them free from the law of sin and death, and because God had done what the law, weakened by our flesh, could never do, sending His own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh and condemning sin in the flesh, that the righteous requirement of the law might be fulfilled in us. He wrote that the Spirit Himself bears witness with our spirit that we are children of God, and if children, then heirs—heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ; that the sufferings of this present time are not worth comparing with the glory that is to be revealed; that the whole creation groans as in the pains of childbirth, waiting for its redemption; and that the Spirit helps us in our weakness, interceding for us with groanings too deep for words. And he gave us the great chain that cannot be broken: that those whom God foreknew He predestined, and those whom He predestined He called, and those whom He called He justified, and those whom He justified He also glorified—every link forged by God, not one of them by us. "If God is for us," Paul asked, "who can be against us? He who did not spare His own Son but gave Him up for us all, how will He not also with Him graciously give us all things?" And he ended in a torrent of triumph that I have clung to in the darkest hours, declaring that neither death nor life, nor angels nor rulers, nor things present nor things to come, nor powers, nor height nor depth, nor anything else in all creation, will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord.

I had walked down from the Mount of Olives on the day He ascended, wondering in my heart how the rescue would ever hold, how a salvation entrusted to men as weak and faithless as we had proved ourselves to be could possibly endure to the end. And here in Paul's letter was the answer, written out in full and in order: it holds because it never rested upon us at all. It rested, from before the foundation of the world, upon the Father who chose us, and the Son who died for us, and the Spirit who seals us; and the God who did not spare His own Son will surely, having given us the greater gift, not fail to give us every lesser one along the way home. I had thought the chain might break at the weakest link, which was me. Paul showed me there was no human link in the chain at all.

When I am afraid—and I have been afraid often in my long life, of men and of prisons and of death and most of all of my own weakness—I go back to the end of the eighth chapter and read it aloud to myself in the dark. Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? Neither death nor life, nor things present nor things to come, nor anything in all creation. I had wondered, on the day He ascended, how the rescue could ever hold, entrusted as it was to men as faithless as we had shown ourselves to be. And here is the answer that has held me through everything: it holds because it does not rest on us at all. The chain that Paul forges—foreknown, predestined, called, justified, glorified—has not a single human link in it; every link is the work of God, and God does not begin a work He will not finish. My salvation is as secure as the faithfulness of God Himself, and no power in heaven or earth or hell can pluck me from the hand that bought me. I had thought the weak link was me. There is no human link at all.

After the uproar in Ephesus had ceased, Paul called the disciples together, encouraged them, and said farewell, and set out for Macedonia, giving the believers there much encouragement as he went, and so came to Greece, where he stayed three months. When a plot against him was discovered as he was about to sail for Syria, he decided to go back through Macedonia instead, and a company of brothers from many of the churches traveled with him, the firstfruits of the very nations he had labored to gather. At Troas we gathered on the first day of the week to break bread, and Paul, intending to depart the next day, talked on and on until midnight, the room warm and close with the smoke of many lamps. A young man named Eutychus, seated in an open window, sank into a deep sleep as Paul talked still longer, and overcome by sleep he fell down from the third story and was taken up dead. But Paul went down, bent over him, and taking him in his arms said, "Do not be alarmed, for his life is in him." And they took the lad away alive and were not a little comforted, and Paul went on talking until dawn and then departed. I smiled when I heard it, for it was the old pattern still at work, unchanged across all the years and miles—life called back through the arms of a servant, just as it had once come through the hands of the Lord at the bedside of Jairus' little girl. Death still let go its hold wherever the name of Jesus and the power of His Spirit were at work.

When I heard of the boy Eutychus, taken up dead from beneath the window and given back alive, I smiled through my tears, for it was so plainly the old pattern still at work. “Tabitha, arise”; “Talitha, cumi”; “Lazarus, come out”; and now a boy in Troas, fallen in the long midnight of Paul's preaching, restored to his weeping friends. Death had been losing its grip, town by town and year by year, ever since the morning the stone was rolled away from the Lord's own tomb. Each of these raisings was but a small token, a firstfruit, a promise in miniature of the great resurrection to come, when the trumpet shall sound and all who sleep in Him shall rise. I have buried many; I shall soon be buried myself; but I lay down my dead, and shall lie down myself, in the certain hope of hearing that same voice say, at the last, “Arise.”

From Miletus Paul sent to Ephesus and called the elders of the church to come to him, for he was hurrying to be at Jerusalem if possible by the day of Pentecost, and he would not take the time to go up to Ephesus itself. When they came, he gave them a farewell that those who heard it never forgot, and that moves me still whenever I think on it. He reminded them how he had served the Lord among them with all humility and with tears and with trials, how he had not shrunk from declaring anything that was profitable, teaching them in public and from house to house, testifying both to Jews and to Greeks of repentance toward God and of faith in our Lord Jesus Christ. And now, he told them, he was going to Jerusalem, bound in the Spirit, not knowing what would happen to him there, except that the Holy Spirit testified in every city that imprisonment and afflictions awaited him. "But I do not account my life of any value nor as precious to myself," he said, "if only I may finish my course and the ministry that I received from the Lord Jesus, to testify to the gospel of the grace of God."

He charged the elders to pay careful attention to themselves and to all the flock, in which the Holy Spirit had made them overseers, to care for the church of God, which He obtained with His own blood. With His own blood—the price of the whole company of the saved, the ransom paid not in silver or gold but in the very life of God's own Son. He warned them that fierce wolves would come in among them, not sparing the flock, and that even from among their own number men would arise speaking twisted things to draw away disciples after them, and he commended them to God and to the word of His grace, which is able to build them up and to give them the inheritance among all those who are sanctified. Then he knelt down and prayed with them all, and there was much weeping, and they fell on Paul's neck and kissed him, grieving most of all over the word he had spoken, that they would not see his face again. And they accompanied him to the ship. I have thought often that there was much of the Lord Himself in that parting—a shepherd warning his sheep against the wolves, loving them to the very end, setting his face toward suffering for the sake of the gospel, exactly as the Master had set His face toward Jerusalem long before, knowing what waited for Him there and going anyway.

I have wept over this farewell more than once, for there is in it the very heart of a true shepherd, and the very shadow of the Good Shepherd Himself. Paul knew he would not see their faces again; he was going up to chains and afflictions; and yet his concern was not for himself but for the flock, for the wolves that would come in among them, for the truth they must guard. He commended them not to his own care, which would soon be taken from them, but to God and to the word of His grace. I have learned from it how a faithful servant of Christ takes his leave: not clinging to his people as though they were his own, but giving them back to the One who bought them with His blood, trusting that the Lord who began the good work in them will keep it to the end, long after every earthly shepherd has been taken away.

So we sailed away from them and came by Cos and Rhodes to Patara, and finding a ship crossing to Phoenicia we went aboard and set sail, sighting Cyprus and passing it on our left, and landed at Tyre. There we found the disciples and stayed seven days, and through the Spirit they kept telling Paul not to go up to Jerusalem; and when our days there were ended, we departed, and they all, with wives and children, accompanied us until we were outside the city, and we knelt down on the beach and prayed and said farewell to one another. We came at last to Caesarea, and stayed in the house of Philip the evangelist, the same Philip who had once preached in Samaria and baptized the Ethiopian on the desert road, now an old companion in the faith. While we were there, a prophet named Agabus came down from Judea, and taking Paul's belt he bound his own feet and hands with it and said, "Thus says the Holy Spirit, 'This is how the Jews at Jerusalem will bind the man who owns this belt and deliver him into the hands of the Gentiles.'"

When we heard this, both we and the people there begged Paul with tears not to go up to Jerusalem. But Paul answered, "What are you doing, weeping and breaking my heart? For I am ready not only to be imprisoned but even to die in Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus." And since he would not be persuaded, we ceased and said, "Let the will of the Lord be done." I recognized that surrender the moment the words were repeated to me, for I had heard its like before, in a garden among the olive trees on the night He was betrayed—not my will, but yours be done. The servant was walking the very path of the Master, his face set toward the city that kills the prophets, choosing the cup that was held out to him rather than the safety his friends pressed upon him. I had learned long since that this kind of obedience is not the absence of fear but the conquest of it by love, and that a man who can say "Let the will of the Lord be done" over his own chains has already won a freedom that no prison can take.

When we came to Jerusalem, the brothers received us gladly, and the next day Paul went in with us to James, and all the elders were present, and Paul related one by one the things that God had done among the Gentiles through his ministry, and they glorified God when they heard it. But there were many thousands of Jewish believers, all zealous for the law, who had been told that Paul taught the Jews among the Gentiles to forsake Moses; and so, to show that there was no truth in it, Paul agreed to join four men in a vow and to pay their expenses in the Temple. But when the seven days were almost completed, the Jews from Asia, seeing Paul in the Temple, stirred up the whole crowd and laid hands on him, crying out, "Men of Israel, help! This is the man who is teaching everyone everywhere against the people and the law and this place"—for they supposed, falsely, that he had brought a Gentile into the Temple. The whole city was aroused, and the people ran together and seized Paul and dragged him out of the Temple, and at once the gates were shut, and they were beating him and trying to kill him when word came up to the Roman tribune that all Jerusalem was in confusion. He came down at once with soldiers and centurions, and the crowd, seeing the soldiers, stopped beating Paul; and the tribune arrested him and ordered him bound with two chains. The mob followed, crying out, "Away with him!"

That cry was so like the one I had heard outside Pilate's hall, the very words the crowd had screamed against the Lord, that a cold shudder ran through me when the report reached me. The disciple was being handed over as his Lord had been—bound, beaten, shouted against by the very people he had come to bless, dragged out of the Temple by the guardians of the Temple. And yet, even as I grieved for him, I knew in my heart that this was not the end of the gospel but its road to Rome. The Lord had already told Paul plainly that he must bear witness also in Rome, and I had learned long before, at the foot of a cross that looked like the death of every hope, that what seems to the eye like the defeat of the word of God is so often the very means by which He sends it farther than it had ever gone. The chains the tribune fastened on Paul's wrists that day were, though none of us could yet see it, the gospel's passage to the heart of the empire.

When the report of his arrest reached me, and I heard that the crowd had dragged him from the Temple crying "Away with him," I sat a long while in grief, for the words were the very words I had heard screamed against the Lord outside Pilate's hall. And I thought: it is happening again, the servant treading the path of the Master. But I have come to see that this is not the tragedy it appears, but the very shape of a life given wholly to Christ. The Lord told us that the servant is not greater than his Master, and that if they persecuted Him they would persecute us. To be handed over, bound, shouted against for His name is not to fall outside His care but to be conformed to His image, to share in His sufferings that we may share in His glory. I no longer pity those of us who are made to walk that road; I have learned to count it, as the apostles did, a thing to rejoice in.

As Paul was about to be brought into the barracks, he asked the tribune leave to speak to the people, and standing on the steps he motioned with his hand, and when there was a great hush he addressed them in the Hebrew tongue. He told them the story of his own life—how he had been brought up in Jerusalem at the feet of Gamaliel, educated strictly in the law, zealous for God as they all were that day; how he had persecuted this Way to the death, binding and delivering to prison both men and women, as the high priest and the whole council of elders could testify. And then he told them of the road to Damascus, the light from heaven brighter than the noonday sun, the voice that named him, "Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me," and the answer, "I am Jesus of Nazareth, whom you are persecuting." He told of Ananias, a devout man according to the law, who had restored his sight and bidden him be baptized and wash away his sins, calling on the name of the Lord. They listened to him until he came to the word the Lord had spoken to him in a trance in the Temple: "Go, for I will send you far away to the Gentiles." At that word they lifted up their voices and cried, "Away with such a fellow from the earth! For he should not be allowed to live," and they shouted and threw off their cloaks and flung dust into the air. The tribune ordered him brought into the barracks and examined by flogging, to learn why they shouted so against him; but as they stretched him out, Paul said to the centurion standing by, "Is it lawful for you to flog a man who is a Roman citizen and uncondemned?" and they drew back in fear, and the tribune was alarmed to find that he had bound a citizen. I marked the strange providence in it: the very citizenship Paul had been born into, in a Gentile city far from Jerusalem, became the shield that preserved his life again and again on the road the Lord had appointed to Rome.

I have noticed how Paul, given the chance to speak for his life, did not argue his innocence or plead for mercy, but told the story of how the Lord had laid hold of him on the Damascus road. Again and again, before mobs and governors and kings, his defense was simply his testimony, what he had been and what the grace of God had made of him. And I have come to see that there is no argument more powerful than a changed life honestly told. Men may dispute our doctrines and resist our reasonings, but they cannot easily explain away a man who once breathed murder against the saints and now would die for them. Paul's whole defense was the gospel written in his own flesh: I was the chief of sinners, and the Lord Jesus had mercy on me. I have learned that when we do not know what else to say for our faith, we may always say that, what we were, and what He has done.

The next day, desiring to know the real reason the Jews accused him, the tribune brought Paul down and set him before the chief priests and all the council—the same Sanhedrin that had condemned the Lord to death. Paul, looking intently at them, said, "Brothers, I have lived my life before God in all good conscience up to this day." At that the high priest Ananias commanded those standing by to strike him on the mouth, and Paul answered, "God is going to strike you, you whitewashed wall! Are you sitting to judge me according to the law, and yet contrary to the law you order me to be struck?" But when he learned it was the high priest, he yielded, citing the Scripture that one must not speak evil of a ruler of the people. Then, perceiving that one part of the council were Sadducees and the other Pharisees, Paul cried out, "Brothers, I am a Pharisee, a son of Pharisees. It is with respect to the hope and the resurrection of the dead that I am on trial." At this a dissension arose between the two parties, for the Sadducees say there is no resurrection, nor angel, nor spirit, but the Pharisees acknowledge them all; and the assembly was divided, and the dispute became so violent that the tribune, fearing Paul would be torn to pieces, ordered the soldiers to take him by force out of their midst and bring him into the barracks. The following night the Lord stood by Paul and said, "Take courage, for as you have testified to the facts about me in Jerusalem, so you must testify also in Rome." I have held to those words ever since, for I had feared greatly for Paul's life in those days; but the Lord Himself stood by His servant in the dark of the cell and gave him not a promise of comfort but a promise of purpose—Rome—and no plot of men, however cunning, could turn Him from it. The bonds that looked to every eye like the end of Paul's work were the very means by which the gospel would be carried, under guard and in chains, to the capital of the world.

When it was day, more than forty of the Jews bound themselves under an oath neither to eat nor drink until they had killed Paul, and they laid their plan before the chief priests, asking that Paul be brought down to the council again, so they might ambush and kill him on the way. But the son of Paul's sister heard of the ambush, and went and told Paul, who sent him to the tribune; and the tribune, learning of the plot, called two centurions and ordered a great guard prepared—two hundred soldiers, seventy horsemen, and two hundred spearmen—to take Paul safely down to Felix the governor at Caesarea by night, with a letter explaining the case. I marveled, when I heard the whole of it, at how the Lord wove even the malice of murderers into the carrying out of His own word. He had said Paul must reach Rome; and so the very plot meant to end his life became the reason he was hurried out of Jerusalem under the protection of nearly five hundred armed men, safe and surrounded, one long stage farther down the road the Lord had appointed for him. I have seen it again and again across my long life, and I never cease to wonder at it: what men intend for the death of the gospel, God bends into its advance. The cross itself had taught me that lesson once and for all—that the worst the enemies of God can do becomes, in His hands, the very instrument of the salvation they meant to stop.

I have seen the hand of God in nothing more clearly than in the way He wove the murderous plot of those forty men into the safe carrying of Paul to Caesarea, surrounded by an army, one stage farther down the very road to Rome that the Lord had appointed. The men who swore not to eat until they had killed him became, all unwilling, the reason he was hurried out of their reach under guard. I have lived long enough to see this a hundred times: that what the enemies of God devise for the ruin of His servants, He turns to their preservation and to the advance of His purpose. Joseph's brothers meant evil and God meant it for good; the council meant to silence the Lord by the cross and instead set the whole world free. I have learned, therefore, not to despair at the schemes of wicked men, for there is no plot so cunning that the Lord cannot bend it, even against the schemers' will, into the doing of His own good pleasure.

Five days later the high priest Ananias came down to Caesarea with some elders and a hired orator named Tertullus, who flattered the governor and laid out a smooth and lying accusation against Paul, calling him a plague, a stirrer-up of riots, a ringleader of the sect of the Nazarenes. But Paul answered for himself plainly, denying that he had stirred up any crowd, and confessing freely the one thing they truly held against him: "But this I confess to you, that according to the Way, which they call a sect, I worship the God of our fathers, believing everything laid down by the Law and written in the Prophets, having a hope in God, which these men themselves accept, that there will be a resurrection of both the just and the unjust." Felix, who had a rather accurate knowledge of the Way, put them off, saying he would decide when the tribune came down. Some days later he sent for Paul and listened to him speak about faith in Christ Jesus; and as Paul reasoned about righteousness and self-control and the coming judgment, Felix was alarmed and said, "Go away for the present. When I get an opportunity I will summon you." He hoped, besides, that money might be given him by Paul, and so he sent for him often and conversed with him. But that opportunity, so far as I ever learned, never came, and after two years, wishing to do the Jews a favor, Felix left Paul in prison.

That trembling governor has stayed in my memory across all the years as a solemn warning. He felt the truth; he was alarmed by it; he saw plainly enough, when Paul spoke of righteousness and self-control and the judgment to come, that he himself stood condemned before God and needed the very mercy that his prisoner was offering him. And he sent the messenger away to a more convenient season that, so far as any of us ever knew, never came. I thought of the rich young ruler who went away sorrowful because he had great possessions, and of the seed that hears the word but is choked by the cares and pleasures of this life. It is a terrible thing to come so near the open door of salvation, to feel its very pull upon the heart, and then to turn back to one's silver and one's comfort and the next convenient hour. The gospel had reached Felix; the gospel had stood bound before him for two long years; and Felix would not come in. For not all who hear are saved—only those who, hearing, come, and Felix kept saying, soon, soon, until the door was shut.

Felix has haunted me across the years as the very picture of the almost-saved, who are in the end the wholly lost. He trembled; he understood; he sent for Paul again and again; and he never once bent his knee. He was waiting, he said, for a convenient season—and I have learned that the convenient season is the great lie by which more souls are lost than by open unbelief. The man who flatly denies the gospel at least knows where he stands; but the man who means to repent later, who feels the truth and puts it off for a more convenient hour, is lulled to sleep at the very door of life and wakes to find it shut. The Spirit does not always strive; the door does not always stand open; the conviction that is stifled today may not return tomorrow. I have begged many a Felix, in my long life, not to wait—for now is the accepted time, and now is the day of salvation, and the soul that says "tomorrow" to God has no promise of a tomorrow.

When Festus succeeded Felix as governor, the Jews of Jerusalem pressed their case against Paul afresh, asking as a favor that he be summoned to Jerusalem—planning, in truth, another ambush on the road. But Festus told them to come down to Caesarea, and there, when they brought many serious charges they could not prove, and Paul answered that he had committed no offense against the law of the Jews, the Temple, or Caesar, Festus, wishing to do the Jews a favor, asked whether Paul would go up to Jerusalem to be tried. Then Paul, knowing well what waited for him on that road, said the words that settled his course: "I appeal to Caesar." And Festus, after conferring with his council, answered, "To Caesar you have appealed; to Caesar you shall go." A few days later King Agrippa and his sister Bernice arrived to greet the new governor, and Festus laid Paul's case before the king, confessing that the dispute was about certain points of the Jews' own religion and about a certain Jesus, who was dead, but whom Paul asserted to be alive. Agrippa said he would like to hear the man himself, and Festus answered, "Tomorrow you shall hear him."

So on the next day Agrippa and Bernice came with great pomp into the audience hall, with the military tribunes and the prominent men of the city, and Paul was brought in—a prisoner in chains before all the splendor of an earthly court. And being given leave to speak, he stretched out his hand and told once more the whole story of his life: his strict upbringing as a Pharisee, his rage against the name of Jesus, how he had shut up many of the saints in prison and cast his vote against them and tried to make them blaspheme, and how, on the road to Damascus at midday, a light brighter than the sun had shone around him, and the voice had said, "Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me? It is hard for you to kick against the goads." He told how the Lord had appointed him a servant and witness, to open the eyes of the Gentiles, to turn them from darkness to light and from the power of Satan to God, that they might receive forgiveness of sins and a place among those who are sanctified by faith in Him. He had not been disobedient to the heavenly vision, Paul said, but had declared everywhere that men should repent and turn to God; and he said nothing but what the prophets and Moses had foretold would come to pass—that the Christ must suffer and that, by being the first to rise from the dead, He would proclaim light both to our people and to the Gentiles.

At this Festus cried out with a loud voice, "Paul, you are out of your mind; your great learning is driving you out of your mind." But Paul answered, "I am not out of my mind, most excellent Festus, but I am speaking true and rational words." And then he turned to the king: "King Agrippa, do you believe the prophets? I know that you believe." And Agrippa said to Paul, "In a short time would you persuade me to be a Christian?" And Paul's reply has never left me, and I think it never will: "Whether short or long, I would to God that not only you but also all who hear me this day might become such as I am—except for these chains." A prisoner in irons, standing before a king and a governor and the great men of the province, wished them every one the freedom that he himself possessed; for he knew, as I have come to know, that the only true bondage in all the world is sin, and the only true liberty is Christ, and that a man may be chained at the wrist and yet be freer in his soul than the king who sits in judgment over him. Agrippa concluded, when they had withdrawn, that this man had done nothing deserving death or imprisonment, and said to Festus, "This man could have been set free if he had not appealed to Caesar." But the appeal was no mistake; it was the Lord's own appointed road to Rome, and the chains Agrippa pitied were the very means by which the gospel would stand at last before the throne of the empire.

I have set that scene before my mind many times—the prisoner in his chains and the king in his pomp—and asked which of the two was truly free. Agrippa sat in purple, with the governor at his side and the great men of the province gathered to do him honor; Paul stood bound, an old man worn by beatings and shipwreck and prison. And yet it was Paul who pitied Agrippa, and not the other way around. "I would to God," he said, "that you were such as I am, except for these chains." He knew, as I have come to know, that the only chains that finally matter are the chains of sin, and the only freedom worth the name is to belong to Christ. A man may sit on a throne and be a slave; a man may stand in irons and be the freest soul in the room. I have envied many things in my life, but I have never since envied a king his crown, having seen a prisoner pity one.

And so they put Paul and some other prisoners aboard a ship under a centurion named Julius, of the Augustan Cohort, and set sail at last for Italy.
