I have heard the account of that voyage many times from those who made it, for it was a tale of terror and of the Lord's faithfulness woven so tightly together that one could not tell them apart. The season for sailing was already dangerous, and Paul warned them that the voyage would bring injury and much loss, not only of the cargo and the ship but of their lives; yet the centurion listened to the captain and the owner rather than to the prisoner, and they put out to sea. Soon a tempestuous wind, the one they call the northeaster, rushed down and struck the ship and drove it before the gale, so that they could not face it and gave way and were driven along. They threw the cargo overboard with their own hands, and then the ship's tackle, and when neither sun nor stars appeared for many days, and no small tempest lay on them, at last all hope of being saved was abandoned.

Then Paul stood up among them, in the howling dark of the hold, and said, "Take heart, for there will be no loss of life among you, but only of the ship. For this very night there stood before me an angel of the God to whom I belong and whom I worship, and he said, 'Do not be afraid, Paul; you must stand before Caesar. And behold, God has granted you all those who sail with you.' So take heart, men, for I have faith in God that it will be exactly as I have been told." After fourteen nights of being driven across the sea, when they sensed land was near, and the sailors tried to abandon ship in the lifeboat, Paul told the centurion, "Unless these men stay in the ship, you cannot be saved," and the soldiers cut the boat away. As day was about to dawn, Paul urged them all to take food, for they had eaten nothing in their long ordeal, and taking bread he gave thanks to God in the presence of all, and broke it and began to eat, and they were all encouraged and took food themselves. Then they ran the ship aground, and the bow stuck fast while the stern was broken up by the surf, and the soldiers planned to kill the prisoners lest any escape; but the centurion, wishing to save Paul, kept them from it, and ordered those who could swim to make for land, and the rest on planks and pieces of the ship. And so it was that all were brought safely to land—two hundred and seventy-six souls, and not one of them lost, exactly as the Lord had promised.

I have loved that voyage, and one small mercy hidden inside the great one above all. For the sake of one man whom the Lord was carrying to Rome to bear witness, He spared the whole shipload—soldiers and sailors and prisoners and all, men who knew nothing of Jesus and had not asked to be saved. So it has always been with those whom God saves: they become a blessing to all who are near them, and the very presence of one of the Lord's servants in the storm becomes the rescue of many who never knew to ask for it. The world little knows how much it owes to the praying few in its midst, the handful for whose sake the ship is spared, as Sodom would have been spared for ten righteous men. Paul broke bread and gave thanks in the teeth of the gale, as the Lord had broken bread on the green hillside and in the upper room, and the breaking of that bread put courage into despairing men—a small foretaste, in the dark of a sinking ship, of the feast at the end of all storms.

I have loved to think on the bread Paul broke in the howling dark of that sinking ship, when all hope had been abandoned and men had not eaten for fourteen days. He took bread, and gave thanks to God in the presence of them all, and broke it, and began to eat—and they were all encouraged. It was such a small thing, a man giving thanks over bread in a storm; and yet it put courage into two hundred and seventy-six despairing souls, because it was the act of a man who plainly believed that God would do what He had promised. I have come to see that this is much of what the Lord's people are for in this storm-tossed world: to give thanks in the dark, to break bread in the teeth of the gale, to act as those who trust the promise when everyone around them has given up hope. The world little knows how much it owes to the quiet, thankful faith of the few in its midst, for whose sake, like Paul's shipmates, it is so often spared.

When they had been brought safely through, they learned that the island was called Malta, and the native people showed them unusual kindness, kindling a fire and welcoming them all because of the rain and the cold. As Paul gathered a bundle of sticks and put them on the fire, a viper came out because of the heat and fastened on his hand. When the natives saw the creature hanging from his hand, they said to one another that this man must be a murderer, who though he had escaped the sea, Justice had not allowed to live. But Paul shook off the creature into the fire and suffered no harm, and when they waited a long time and saw no misfortune come to him, they changed their minds and said he was a god. Nearby were the lands of the chief man of the island, named Publius, whose father lay sick with fever and dysentery; and Paul visited him and prayed and laid his hands on him and healed him. After that the rest of the sick on the island came and were cured, and they honored the company greatly and provided for their needs. After three months they set sail in a ship that had wintered in the island, and came by Syracuse and Rhegium to Puteoli, where they found brothers and stayed seven days; and so at last they came toward Rome. And the believers there, hearing of their coming, came out as far as the Forum of Appius and the Three Taverns to meet them, and when Paul saw them, he thanked God and took courage. I have always been touched by that—that after the trial and the storm and the long captivity, what put fresh heart into Paul was simply the sight of his brothers walking out along the road to meet him. The fellowship of the saints is itself a mercy from God, a foretaste of the great gathering to come.

I have always been touched by the small detail that what put fresh heart into Paul, after the trial and the storm and the long captivity, was simply the sight of his brothers coming out along the road to meet him at the Forum of Appius and the Three Taverns. He had faced down mobs and councils and the open sea without flinching; and it was the faces of fellow believers walking out to greet him that made him thank God and take courage. I have learned from it not to despise the simple fellowship of the saints, nor to think it a small thing. We were made to bear one another up, to be Christ's hands and face to one another in a hard world; and the company of those who love the same Lord is itself one of His sweetest mercies, a foretaste even now of the great gathering to come, when we shall all meet on the far shore and never part again.

And when Paul came to Rome, he was allowed to stay by himself, with a soldier to guard him. After three days he called together the local leaders of the Jews and explained that he had done nothing against his people, and that it was because of the hope of Israel that he wore this chain. They came to him in great numbers at his lodging, and from morning till evening he expounded to them, testifying to the kingdom of God and trying to convince them about Jesus from the Law of Moses and from the Prophets. Some were convinced, and some disbelieved, and when they disagreed among themselves and departed, Paul declared that this salvation of God had been sent to the Gentiles, and they would listen. And he lived there two whole years at his own expense, and welcomed all who came to him, proclaiming the kingdom of God and teaching about the Lord Jesus Christ with all boldness and without hindrance.

There, with those words, the account of all these journeys, as it has been written down for us, comes to its rest—not at Paul's death, not at his release, not at any tidy ending, but with the gospel sounding out freely in the very heart of the empire, from a prisoner's rented lodging, through chains that could bind the man but could not bind the word of God. I have thought there could be no fitter place to pause the story. The Lord had told us on the Mount of Olives, before He was taken up, that we would be His witnesses in Jerusalem, in all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth; and here, in one generation, the word had traveled from a manger in Bethlehem and a carpenter's bench in Nazareth, through Galilee and Jerusalem and Samaria, through Antioch and Cyprus and Athens and Corinth and Ephesus, across the sea and through the shipwreck, all the way to Rome itself, the head and heart of the whole world—and still it was going out, still saving, still unhindered, still unstoppable. What had begun with one Man calling fishermen by the shore of a Galilean lake had become a fire spreading across the nations, and no power of Rome or of hell had been able to put it out.

I have always thought it fitting that the great account of the church's birth ends not with a triumph or a tragedy but with an open door and an unhindered word—the gospel sounding freely from a prisoner's lodging in the heart of the empire. For the story was not finished, and is not finished still. The book breaks off, but the word goes on. The Lord told us we would be His witnesses to the end of the earth, and the end had not yet come, nor has it now; the gospel that reached Rome in chains has reached lands the apostles never dreamed of, and is reaching them yet. I am one of the last of those who saw Him; soon I too will be gone. But the witness will not be gone, for the word of the Lord endures forever, and the door He has opened no man can shut, and the salvation that began by a Galilean lake will not cease until the last of His people, from every nation, is gathered home.
§§ Ephesians

From his imprisonment in Rome, Paul wrote letters that have become among the most precious treasures of the whole church, and the first of them I would name is the one to the Ephesians, though I think he meant it to be shared among many of the churches of Asia. In it he soared higher into the wonders of our salvation than I had ever heard any man go, and reading it is like standing at the foot of a mountain and craning one's neck to find the summit. He began not with us at all but with God, blessing the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ who has blessed us in Christ with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places, even as He chose us in Him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and blameless before Him; who in love predestined us for adoption as sons through Jesus Christ, according to the purpose of His will, to the praise of His glorious grace, with which He has blessed us in the Beloved. In Him we have redemption through His blood, the forgiveness of our trespasses, according to the riches of His grace. I marveled, reading it, that the rescue I had watched unfold in time and dust and blood on the roads of Galilee and on the hill of Golgotha had in truth been settled in the very heart of God before ever the world was made—that I had been chosen in Christ before there was a sun to rise or a sea to roar.

But the words of his that I have read most often, until I know them as well as my own breath, are these: "For by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God, not a result of works, so that no one may boast." There it was again, the truth that the whole gospel had been pressing into me from the very first day by the Jordan—that we are saved by a gift we did not earn and never could earn, lest any man stand before God and claim even the smallest portion of the credit for his own rescue. Paul wrote that we were once dead in the trespasses and sins in which we walked, children of wrath like the rest of mankind; but God, being rich in mercy, because of the great love with which He loved us, even when we were dead in our trespasses, made us alive together with Christ, and raised us up with Him, and seated us with Him in the heavenly places. Dead men do not raise themselves; a corpse contributes nothing whatever to its own resurrection. I thought of Lazarus called out of the tomb, of Jairus' daughter, of the widow's son at Nain, of Tabitha in the upper room at Joppa, and I saw that what the Lord had done to their bodies, He does to every dead soul that He saves: He speaks, and the dead hear, and live. And Paul wrote of the wall thrown down—that Christ Himself is our peace, who has made Jew and Gentile both into one, breaking down in His flesh the dividing wall of hostility, that He might create in Himself one new man in place of the two, so making peace, and reconcile us both to God in one body through the cross. The veil of the Temple torn from top to bottom, the wall of hostility thrown down, the far-off brought near by the blood of Christ—it was all of one piece, the gathering of the one new family of God by the blood of the one Lamb.

I have stood at the foot of this letter as at the foot of a great mountain, straining to see the summit, and I have never reached it. That God should have chosen me in Christ before the foundation of the world, before there was a sea to roar or a star to shine—that the rescue I watched unfold in dust and blood was settled in the heart of God before time began—this is too high for me, and I can only worship. And yet Paul does not leave it in the heavens; he brings it down to the dust where I live, and tells me that I, who was dead, have been made alive, and raised, and seated with Christ in the heavenly places already, even now. I am a poor old man with shaking hands; and I am seated with Christ in glory. Both are true at once, and the second is the truer, for it rests not on what I am but on where He is, and I am in Him. Grace from first to last, that no man may boast, and that every mouth, in the end, may be filled only with His praise.
§§ Philippians

To the church at Philippi—the church that had begun with Lydia by the riverside and the jailer who fell trembling and asked how to be saved—Paul wrote a letter overflowing with joy, though he wrote it in chains, not knowing whether he would live to see them again or die under Caesar's sword. "For to me to live is Christ," he wrote, "and to die is gain," and I knew he meant every word of it, for I had heard how he and Silas had sung hymns in that very city's prison with their backs torn open. He told them that what had happened to him had really served to advance the gospel, so that his imprisonment for Christ had become known throughout the whole imperial guard, and that he rejoiced, and would rejoice, whether by life or by death Christ was honored in his body.

At the very heart of the letter he set down words that have shaped my own soul more than I can say—a hymn, it seemed, of the church, telling how Christ Jesus, though He was in the form of God, did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied Himself, taking the form of a servant, being born in the likeness of men; and being found in human form, He humbled Himself by becoming obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross; and therefore God has highly exalted Him and bestowed on Him the name that is above every name, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father. I read it and saw the whole arc of the One I had followed laid out in a few short lines: the glory laid aside, the basin and the towel and the washing of our feet, the cup in the garden, the cross, the empty tomb, the cloud on the mountain, and the throne. The road down and the road up; the descent into the depths of our death and the ascent to the highest place in heaven—it was all there, and Paul sang it not only as the story of our salvation but as the very pattern for our own humility, bidding us count others more significant than ourselves. And Paul, the former Pharisee who had once trusted in his blameless pedigree and his zeal for the law, counted all of it as loss, as rubbish, that he might gain Christ and be found in Him, not having a righteousness of his own that comes from the law, but the righteousness from God that depends on faith—that he might know Him and the power of His resurrection and share in His sufferings. The man who had once trusted everything in himself now boasted in nothing at all but Christ, and pressed on toward the prize of the upward call of God, and bade us rejoice in the Lord always, and again he said, rejoice, for the Lord is at hand.

I have made that hymn my own meditation through many years—the road down and the road up, the descent of the Son into our death and His ascent to the throne. And I have seen that Paul set it before us not only to be adored but to be imitated: have this mind among yourselves, he said, which is yours in Christ Jesus. The Lord who was in the form of God did not grasp at His rights but emptied Himself and took the form of a servant and humbled Himself to death; and we who follow Him are to walk that same downward road, counting others more significant than ourselves, seeking not our own. The world climbs; the Christian descends, as his Master descended, and finds at the bottom that this is the only road that leads, at the last, to being lifted up. I have watched proud men ruin themselves grasping at greatness, and humble men shine like the Lord Himself; and I have learned that in His kingdom the way up is always down.
§§ Colossians

To the Colossians, a church he had not himself founded but loved nonetheless, Paul wrote to guard them against teachers who would diminish Christ—who would add to Him their philosophies and their rules about food and festivals and their worship of angels, as though He alone were not sufficient, as though a believer needed something more than the Lord Himself to be complete. And so Paul lifted up the Lord in words of such surpassing majesty that I have never tired of them. He is the image of the invisible God, Paul wrote, the firstborn of all creation, for by Him all things were created, in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones or dominions or rulers or authorities—all things were created through Him and for Him. And He is before all things, and in Him all things hold together. And He is the head of the body, the church; He is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, that in everything He might be preeminent. For in Him all the fullness of God was pleased to dwell, and through Him to reconcile to Himself all things, whether on earth or in heaven, making peace by the blood of His cross.

I drank in those words, for they set my Lord where He belongs—above all, before all, holding all things together by the word of His power, the very One I had watched still a storm with a word, and break five loaves to feed a multitude, and weep at the tomb of His friend. Paul wrote that we who were once alienated and hostile in mind, doing evil deeds, have now been reconciled in His body of flesh by His death, to be presented holy and blameless and above reproach before God. He spoke of the record of debt that stood against us with its legal demands, which God set aside, nailing it to the cross—and I thought of the charge that had been fixed above the Lord's head at Golgotha, naming the crime for which He was condemned, and I saw that the true charge nailed there was not His crime at all but mine, the long and damning list of my own sins, cancelled forever in His dying, the handwriting against me blotted out. And Paul named the mystery hidden for ages and generations but now revealed to the saints, which is "Christ in you, the hope of glory." The Savior who had once walked beside me on the dusty roads of Galilee now dwelt within His people by His Spirit, the very Helper poured out at Pentecost, and that indwelling was the surest pledge and down payment that the glory begun in us would surely be brought to its appointed end.

It has been my comfort in old age that Paul names the great mystery of the gospel as "Christ in you, the hope of glory." For the Lord whom I once walked beside on the roads of Galilee, whose face I saw and whose voice I heard and whose feet I watched gather the dust, is no longer beside me in the body; the cloud took Him long ago. And yet He is nearer to me now than He was even then, for by His Spirit He dwells within me, and within all His people, the very Helper He promised in the upper room. The disciples who walked with Him in the flesh had Him beside them; we who believe now have Him within us, which the Lord Himself said was the better thing. And this indwelling is the down payment, the first installment, the sure pledge of the glory to come; for the One who has joined Himself to me so closely will not let me go, but will bring the work He has begun in me to its appointed end, when I shall see Him face to face.
§§ Philemon

The shortest of all the letters that Paul sent out from his Roman chains was to a man named Philemon, and it concerned a runaway slave named Onesimus, who had wronged his master and fled, and who had somehow found his way to Paul in prison, and there found Christ. Paul was sending him back to his master, no longer as a slave only but as a beloved brother, and he pleaded for him with the tenderest words, offering even to pay out of his own pocket whatever the slave had stolen or owed: "If he has wronged you at all, or owes you anything, charge that to my account. I, Paul, write this with my own hand: I will repay it."

I have always thought that this little letter holds the whole gospel within it, like a single drop of water that carries the taste of the whole sea. For here was a debtor who could not pay his debt, received back not on the ground of his own worth—he had none to plead—but for the sake of another who stood as surety for him, with all that he owed charged to an innocent account and paid by an innocent hand. And is this not exactly, precisely, what the Lord Jesus has done for me? I had run from God as Onesimus ran from his master; I had wronged Him and robbed Him and owed Him a debt I could never in ten thousand years repay. And the Lord Jesus had stepped between me and the reckoning, and said to the Father, in effect, "Charge that to my account—I will repay it," and had paid it not with silver or gold but with His own blood, that I might be received back no longer as a runaway slave but as a beloved son and brother. Paul asked Philemon to welcome Onesimus exactly as he would welcome Paul himself; and the Father welcomes us exactly as He welcomes His own beloved Son, because we come to Him clothed in that Son, and counted in Him. The mercy I had watched poured out from the cross was now, in a small house in Asia, teaching a slaveowner and his runaway to live as brothers in Christ; and in the reconciling of those two men, I saw the picture of my own.
§§ 1 Timothy

Paul, it seems, was released from that first Roman imprisonment, and for a season he traveled again among the churches before the end came upon him. From those years came his letters to Timothy and to Titus, the young men he had left to shepherd the flocks at Ephesus and on Crete—letters of a father to his sons in the faith, full of charges to guard sound doctrine, to appoint faithful elders, to rebuke error gently and to keep themselves pure. To Timothy at Ephesus he wrote first, warning him against those who wanted to be teachers of the law without understanding it, and reminding him that the law is good if one uses it lawfully, that it is laid down not for the righteous but for the lawless and the ungodly, to drive sinners to the grace that alone can save them.

And then Paul set down what he called a trustworthy saying, deserving of full acceptance, and I have copied it out and kept it where my eyes fall on it often: "Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the foremost." I loved Paul for that confession when I first heard it, and I love him for it still. The apostle who had carried the gospel across the world, who had been caught up to the third heaven, who had written the great letter to the Romans setting out the whole counsel of God—he still called himself the foremost of sinners, the chief of them, and counted his own salvation the prime exhibit of the Lord's perfect patience, a pattern set up for all who would afterward believe. The man who had held the coats at Stephen's stoning never once got over the wonder of having been forgiven. And neither, I have found, do any of us who have truly grasped what we were and what we have been given. Grace does not make a man forget his debt; it makes him treasure forever the One who paid it. He charged Timothy to wage the good warfare, to fight the good fight of the faith, to take hold of the eternal life to which he was called, and to keep the commandment unstained until the appearing of our Lord Jesus Christ, whom God will display at the proper time—He who alone has immortality, who dwells in unapproachable light, to whom be honor and eternal dominion.

I have copied out that trustworthy saying and kept it where my eyes fall on it daily, for it is the whole gospel in eight words: Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners. And I have loved that Paul added, "of whom I am the foremost"—not "of whom I was," in his persecuting days, but "of whom I am," still, now, in his old age and apostleship. He never graduated from being a saved sinner; none of us does. I have known men who, having walked with Christ many years, came to think themselves advanced beyond the simple gospel, as though grace were the doorway one passes through and then leaves behind. But the saints who shone brightest, in all my long life, were always those who, like Paul, never got over being forgiven, who lived and died as chief of sinners saved by grace. The gospel is not the porch of the house; it is the house itself, and we never move out of it, but only deeper in.
§§ Titus

To Titus, whom he had left on the island of Crete to set in order what remained and to appoint elders in every town, Paul wrote much the same charge, that an overseer must be above reproach, holding firm to the trustworthy word as taught, that the people might be sound in the faith and adorn the doctrine of God our Savior in all they did. But woven through the practical counsel are two passages that gather up the whole of the gospel, and I have treasured them as much as anything Paul ever wrote. "For the grace of God has appeared," he wrote, "bringing salvation for all people, training us to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions, and to live self-controlled, upright, and godly lives in the present age, waiting for our blessed hope, the appearing of the glory of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ, who gave Himself for us to redeem us from all lawlessness and to purify for Himself a people for His own possession, who are zealous for good works."

The grace of God has appeared. It had appeared to me first by the muddy Jordan, in the form of a man with dust on His sandals, and John crying, "Behold, the Lamb of God"; and that same grace had given itself, on a cross, to redeem a people for God's own possession. And Paul wrote, as if he could not help returning to it again and again, of how God our Savior saved us—"not because of works done by us in righteousness, but according to His own mercy, by the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit, whom He poured out on us richly through Jesus Christ our Savior, so that being justified by His grace we might become heirs according to the hope of eternal life." Not because of works done by us in righteousness, but according to His own mercy. I never tired of hearing it, in whatever words it came, from whatever mouth, for it was the one note that the whole gospel sounded from beginning to end, and the note my own soul most needed to hear: that I was saved by His mercy, and not by my own goodness, and could rest there forever.

I have returned often to that word Paul wrote to Titus: that we are saved not because of works done by us in righteousness, but according to His own mercy. There is no sweeter sentence for a dying man to rest his soul upon. For when I come to the end and look back over my long life, I can find no righteousness of my own fit to set before God, only failures forgiven, and grace upon grace. If my salvation rested on my works, I should despair; but it rests on His mercy, and His mercy does not fail. I have watched men try to build their hope on their own goodness, and I have watched that hope crumble at the hour of death when they most needed it; for our best works are stained, and we know it in our hearts. But the man who has learned to say that he is saved not by his own righteousness but by His mercy has a hope that the grave cannot shake, for it rests on the unshakable mercy of God.
§§ 1 Peter

In those same years, before the great fire and the persecution that followed, a letter came from Peter, written to the believers scattered as exiles through the provinces of Asia, who were suffering grief and reproach for the name of Christ. I knew Peter's voice in every line of it—the same voice that had once denied the Lord by a fire of coals and then, restored on a beach by another fire, had stood up at Pentecost and preached three thousand into the kingdom. He wrote to people under fire, and he did the very thing a true shepherd does: he lifted their eyes off their pain and onto their hope.

"Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ," he began, "who according to His great mercy has caused us to be born again to a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead, to an inheritance that is imperishable, undefiled, and unfading, kept in heaven for you, who by God's power are being guarded through faith for a salvation ready to be revealed in the last time." Born again to a living hope—the very thing the Lord had spoken of to Nicodemus by night, that a man must be born again to see the kingdom, now the settled and guarded possession of suffering exiles, secured forever by the empty tomb and kept for them in heaven where no enemy could reach it. Peter reminded them that they had been ransomed from the futile ways inherited from their fathers not with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ, like that of a lamb without blemish or spot. And he wrote of the Lord's suffering in words that I am sure he learned by standing near the cross and never being able to forget what he saw: "He Himself bore our sins in His body on the tree, that we might die to sin and live to righteousness. By His wounds you have been healed. For you were straying like sheep, but have now returned to the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls." I thought of the Lamb of God whom John had pointed out at the Jordan on the first day, of the lamb led to slaughter in Isaiah's song that the Ethiopian had read in his chariot, and I saw the whole long testimony come together in Peter's lines: that Jesus is the spotless Lamb, and His blood the only ransom, and by His wounds we who were straying sheep are healed and brought home to the Shepherd. Peter told the exiles not to be surprised at the fiery trial that came upon them, as though something strange were happening, but to rejoice insofar as they shared Christ's sufferings, and to cast all their anxieties upon Him, because He cares for them.

I knew Peter, and I tell you that the man who wrote "He Himself bore our sins in His body on the tree" had stood near enough to that tree to see the body and the blood, and had never been able to forget it. There is a weight in his words that comes only from having been there. And there is a tenderness, too, that comes from having been forgiven much; for this was the man who had denied the Lord with curses and been restored by a look of love and a breakfast on the shore. When he calls the Lord "the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls," and reminds the scattered, suffering exiles that they were straying sheep now returned, he is speaking out of his own straying and his own return. I have always trusted the comfort of a wounded comforter more than the counsel of one who has never fallen; and Peter, who had fallen so far and been raised so gently, knew exactly how to bind up the wounds of a frightened and failing flock.
§§ Hebrews

About this time there came among us a letter—I never learned with certainty whose hand had written it—addressed to Hebrew believers who, under the weight of persecution, were sorely tempted to slip back into the old religion of priests and sacrifices and the Temple, as though the shadows were safer than the substance that had cast them. It is a letter of surpassing richness, and it does for the whole old covenant what the Lord Himself did on the road to Emmaus: it opens the Scriptures and shows that every part of them was pointing forward to Him.

It declares that God, who long ago at many times and in many ways spoke to our fathers by the prophets, has in these last days spoken to us by His Son, whom He appointed the heir of all things, through whom also He created the world; who is the radiance of the glory of God and the exact imprint of His nature, who upholds the universe by the word of His power; and who, after making purification for sins, sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high. He sat down—and that one detail, when I first marked it, went through me like light. For the priests of the old covenant stood daily at their service, offering again and again the same sacrifices, which could never take away sins; the work was never finished, and so the priest could never sit. But Christ, having offered for all time a single sacrifice for sins, sat down at the right hand of God, because there was nothing left to do, nothing left to add, the work complete and the debt paid in full and forever. The letter calls Him our great high priest, who is also Himself the offering—the one who passed through the heavens, who entered the holy places not by means of the blood of goats and calves but by means of His own blood, thus securing an eternal redemption. He has no need, like the old high priests, to offer sacrifices day after day, first for His own sins and then for the people's, for this He did once for all when He offered up Himself.

The word in this letter that has steadied me most is that small one: He sat down. The priests of old never sat, for their work was never done; they stood day after day, year after year, offering the same sacrifices that could never take away sins, an endless labor that could never reach an end. But Christ, having offered Himself once for all, sat down at the right hand of God, and in that sitting down is all my rest. The work of my salvation is finished; there is nothing left for me to add, nothing left to be done, no sacrifice to repeat, no debt outstanding. I do not labor to be saved; I rest in a salvation already accomplished and a Savior already seated. I have known restless souls who could never believe the work was truly done, who kept trying to add their own offerings to His, and they never found peace. But He is seated; the work is finished; and the weary soul that believes it may at last sit down too, and rest.
§§ Hebrews (continued)

And the letter speaks of the curtain, and of this I have pondered most of all. I had been told, by those who were near, how at the very moment the Lord cried out and gave up His spirit on the cross, the great veil of the Temple, the heavy curtain that shut off the Most Holy Place where the presence of God dwelt, was torn in two from top to bottom, by no human hand, so that what no man had ever been allowed to enter save the high priest once a year, and that not without blood, stood suddenly open. And here, at last, this letter named what that tearing meant: "Therefore, brothers, since we have confidence to enter the holy places by the blood of Jesus, by the new and living way that He opened for us through the curtain, that is, through His flesh, let us draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith." The veil was His flesh, torn open on the cross, that we might come in—come all the way in, into the very presence of God, not trembling at a distance as our fathers had, but with confidence and full assurance, washed clean and welcomed.

I sat a long while with that when I first understood it, and I weep over it still. Every sacrifice I had ever watched smoke up from the altar in my childhood, every Passover lamb whose blood was smeared on the doorposts, every drop of blood the high priest carried behind the veil on the great day of atonement—every one of them had been a finger pointing forward across the centuries to the one true Lamb, whose single offering of Himself would never need to be repeated, and whose torn flesh would open the way to God that all the rivers of animal blood could never open. "It is finished," the Lord had cried from the cross, and this whole letter is but the long and glorious unfolding of those three words. The shadows had served their purpose and were passing away; the substance had come; and the way into the holiest place of all stood open, watered with the blood of the Son of God, for any sinner who would draw near through Him. The letter urged the wavering Hebrews, therefore, not to go back to the shadows, not to shrink back to destruction, but to hold fast their confession and to run with endurance the race set before them, looking to Jesus, the founder and perfecter of our faith, who for the joy set before Him endured the cross, despising the shame, and is seated at the right hand of the throne of God.

I cannot write of that torn veil without my old eyes filling, for I have lived my whole life on the far side of a thing my fathers could only long for. They worshiped at a distance, behind a curtain none might pass; the high priest went in but once a year, trembling, and not without blood, and the people waited outside. And now, because His flesh was torn, the curtain is torn, and the way stands open—not for a priest once a year, but for any sinner, any day, at any hour, to come all the way in, into the very presence of God, with confidence and full assurance. I have come boldly to that throne ten thousand times in my long life, in joy and in grief and in fear, and have never once been turned away, because I do not come in my own name or my own righteousness but in the blood of Jesus, by the new and living way He opened for me. The veil that shut us out is the flesh that was torn to let us in.
§§ 2 Peter

Before the end came upon him, Peter wrote a second letter, sent out, he said, as one who knew that the putting off of his body would be soon, as the Lord Jesus had made clear to him—a last word from a dying shepherd to the flock he loved. He wrote to stir up their minds by way of reminder, that they might remember the words of the prophets and the commandment of the Lord given through the apostles, and that they might grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. He testified that he and the others had not followed cleverly devised myths when they made known the power and coming of the Lord, but had been eyewitnesses of His majesty—and here he spoke of the mountain, of the day he and James and John and I had heard the voice from the cloud and seen the Lord's face shine like the sun, and I knew the truth of every word, for I had been at its foot. He warned sharply against false teachers who would secretly bring in destructive heresies, even denying the Master who bought them, and who would entice unsteady souls with sensuality and greed.

But the deepest comfort of that letter, the part I have leaned on most as the years stretched long and the Lord did not yet return, was Peter's answer to the scoffers. For there were those, even then, who mocked, saying, "Where is the promise of His coming? For ever since the fathers fell asleep, all things are continuing as they were from the beginning of creation." And Peter answered that the Lord is not slow to fulfill His promise as some count slowness, but is patient toward us, not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance. I have held that close, for I am very old now, and many long years have passed since the cloud took Him from the Mount of Olives, and still we wait, and still the scoffers ask their question. But I have learned, through all the waiting, that the long delay is not forgetfulness, nor weakness, nor any failure of His promise; it is mercy, and nothing else but mercy. Every day that He tarries is another day given for one more sinner to come home—another prodigal still on the long road back, another Saul still riding toward Damascus, another dying thief who has not yet turned his head to ask to be remembered. The very patience that has so tried our waiting is the patience that is saving the world, soul by soul. And Peter promised that the day of the Lord will come like a thief, and the heavens will pass away with a roar, and that we, according to His promise, are waiting for new heavens and a new earth in which righteousness dwells.

I have leaned on Peter's word about the Lord's patience more and more as the years have lengthened and the scoffers' question has grown louder: where is the promise of His coming? I do not have all the answers to that question, but I have the one that matters: He is not slow, He is patient; the delay is not forgetfulness but mercy. Every year He tarries is a year in which more of the lost are gathered in, more prodigals coming up the road, more Sauls struck down on the way to Damascus, more dying thieves turning their heads at the last to ask to be remembered. If He had come in my youth, how many now in the kingdom would have been shut out? The waiting that so tries our patience is the very mercy that is saving the world, soul by soul. And so I have learned to be glad even in the delay, and to use the days He gives in telling what I have seen, that one more might come home before the door is shut.
§§ Jude

About the same time there came a short and fiery letter from Jude, another of the Lord's own brothers, who like James had once not believed and now called himself a servant of Jesus Christ. He had set out, he said, to write to us about our common salvation, but had found it needful instead to write urging the believers to contend for the faith that was once for all delivered to the saints, for certain ungodly men had crept in unnoticed, perverting the grace of our God into sensuality and denying our only Master and Lord, Jesus Christ. He warned them with stern examples from of old—of the people saved out of Egypt and afterward destroyed for their unbelief, of the angels who did not keep their proper place, of Sodom and Gomorrah—that grace is never a license to sin, and that those who turn the mercy of God into an excuse for wickedness show that they never understood it at all. But he ended not in warning but in glory, with a doxology I have prayed over more times than I can count, and that I would have spoken over me at my own end: "Now to Him who is able to keep you from stumbling and to present you blameless before the presence of His glory with great joy, to the only God, our Savior, through Jesus Christ our Lord, be glory, majesty, dominion, and authority, before all time and now and forever. Amen." He is able to keep us. Not we ourselves, who stumble and deny and fall asleep in the garden and flee in the dark—but He is able to keep us, and to present us at the last blameless and with great joy. The keeping, like the saving, is His.

I have prayed Jude's closing words over myself more times than I can number, especially now as my strength fails: that He is able to keep me from stumbling, and to present me blameless before the presence of His glory with great joy. For I know my own weakness too well to trust in my own keeping. I have stumbled often in my long life; I fled in the garden; I have feared and failed and doubted. If my standing before God depended on my holding fast to Him, I should have been lost long ago. But the gospel does not say that I must keep myself; it says that He is able to keep me, and to present me at the last not merely acquitted but blameless, and not grudgingly but with great joy. The keeping is His, as the saving was His; and the same hand that laid hold of me by the Jordan will hold me fast through the valley of the shadow and set me at last, faultless and glad, before His glory.
§§ 2 Timothy

The last letter of Paul's that ever reached us was his second to Timothy, written from a cold Roman cell in the time of Nero's cruelty, when to be a Christian had become a crime punished by fire and the sword and the wild beasts. Paul knew the end was upon him now; this was no imprisonment from which he expected release. "For I am already being poured out as a drink offering," he wrote, "and the time of my departure has come. I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith. Henceforth there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, will award to me on that day, and not only to me but also to all who have loved His appearing."

I have never been able to read those words without weeping. The man who counted himself the foremost of sinners, saved by nothing but sheer grace, came to the very end of his course boasting not in his own righteousness, which he had long ago counted rubbish, but in the crown that the righteous Judge would give him—a crown of righteousness that was itself, like everything else from first to last, a gift and never a wage. He told Timothy that he was lonely, that all had deserted him at his first defense, that only Luke was with him, and he asked him to come before winter and to bring the cloak he had left at Troas, and the books, and above all the parchments—an old man, cold and alone in a dungeon, still wanting his books and his Scriptures. He charged Timothy to preach the word in season and out of season, to endure suffering, to do the work of an evangelist, to fulfill his ministry. And then, so far as we ever heard, the executioner came, and Paul, a Roman citizen, was taken outside the walls of the city and beheaded with the sword.

This last letter of Paul's is, to me, the most moving of them all—not for its doctrine, though that is glorious, but for the man I see in it: old, cold, abandoned by nearly all, alone in a dungeon with the executioner's sword soon to fall, asking only for his cloak and his books and his friend before winter. And yet there is no whining in it, no bitterness, no doubt—only "I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith," and the certain hope of a crown laid up by the righteous Judge. I have thought often that a man's faith is most truly shown not in his vigor but in his dying, and that Paul's quiet, unshaken peace in that cell preached the gospel as loudly as any of his sermons. He was being poured out as a drink offering, and he poured gladly, for he knew the One in whom he had believed, and was persuaded that He was able to keep what had been entrusted to Him until that day. I should like to die as Paul died.
§§ The Martyrdoms of Peter and Paul

In those same burning years, Peter too was put to death in Rome, and they say he was crucified, and that he asked to be hung head downward upon the cross, counting himself unworthy to die in the same manner as his Lord had died. And so the two great pillars of the church, the apostle to the Jews and the apostle to the Gentiles, went home to the Lord within a little while of one another, and the church wept for them as for fathers. Yet we did not weep as those who have no hope, for we knew well where they had gone, and to whom. The Lord had told Peter long before, by the charcoal fire on the beach where He had restored him, the kind of death by which he would glorify God; and Peter, who had once fled and denied and wept bitterly, now followed the Shepherd all the way through the valley of the shadow, as James the brother of John had before him, as Stephen had before them all, as so many were doing in those terrible years. I had watched, over a long life, the frightened men of the upper room become men who could sing in prison and rejoice to suffer dishonor for the name and walk steadily to their own crosses, and I knew that nothing on earth had wrought such a change but the salvation that had laid hold of them—for no man dies like that for a tale he knows to be false, or for a hope he is not sure of. They had seen the risen Lord, and death had lost its terror, because they knew, as I knew, the One who had already conquered it.

When the news of their deaths reached me, I grieved as a man grieves for his own brothers, for so they were; and yet, even in the grief, there was a strange and steadying joy, for I knew they had not lost their lives but found them, exactly as the Lord had said. I remembered Peter as I had first known him—the rough, impulsive fisherman who blurted out whatever came to him, who sank in the waves the moment he looked away from the Lord, who swore by the fire that he never knew the man. And I marveled at what grace had made of him: a rock indeed, who followed his Master to a cross and asked to hang head downward, unworthy, he said, to die as his Lord had died. No man is born able to die like that. It is the work of the salvation that lays hold of cowards and makes them martyrs, that takes a man who fled in the garden and gives him, at the last, the courage to glorify God with his death. I had watched it happen in Peter over a lifetime, and it was the surest proof I ever saw that the gospel is true.
§§ The Fall of Jerusalem

Then came the war, and the thing the Lord had wept over from the Mount of Olives came at last to pass. The armies of Rome surrounded Jerusalem, and after a long and terrible siege, with horrors within the walls that I cannot bring myself to write, the city fell, and the Temple was burned to the ground, and not one stone was left standing upon another, exactly as He had foretold to us as we sat looking down upon its golden splendor. When the news reached me I wept, as He had wept—for the city I had loved, for the holy house in whose courts I had worshiped since I was a child, for the people who had not known the time of their visitation nor the things that made for their peace.

But I understood, in a way that I could not have understood in my younger years, what the destruction truly meant. The true Temple had already been destroyed and raised—His body, torn down at Golgotha and raised on the third morning, the temple He had spoken of in the very first days when He said, "Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up." The dwelling place of God was no longer a house of stone upon a hill, to which the nations must come up; it was the Lord Himself, and His people, in whom His Spirit had come to dwell, scattered now through every city of the world. The veil had been torn; the sacrifices had found their end in the one true Sacrifice; and so the shadow passed away, in fire and ruin, precisely because the substance had come and would remain forever. The old order, which had served its purpose and pointed faithfully to Christ, was folded up like a worn-out garment; and the new and living way stood open, no longer in one city only, but to the ends of the earth.

I was old when the city fell, and the news of it broke something in me, for I had loved Jerusalem—had gone up to her feasts as a boy, had worshiped in the Temple courts, had walked her streets with the Lord Himself. And now not one stone stood upon another, just as He had foretold with tears as we sat looking down upon her golden splendor. But in my grief I came to understand what the ruin meant. The Temple had been a great signpost, pointing all our history toward the One who was to come; and now that He had come, and died, and risen, the signpost had done its work, and the sacrifices that pointed to His sacrifice had found their end in Him. The veil was already torn; the true Lamb had already been slain; the dwelling place of God was no longer a house of stone but the risen Christ and His people. The signpost was taken down because the travelers had reached the destination. I wept for the stones, but I worshiped the One the stones had always been pointing to, who can never be thrown down.
§§ The Writing of the Gospels

In those same years, as the war scattered us and the eyewitnesses began one by one to die, the Lord moved His servants to set down in writing what we had seen and heard, lest the testimony be lost when the last of us was gone. Mark, who had once turned back from the work in Pamphylia and been restored, set down the account he had heard from Peter's own lips, plain and swift and vivid. Matthew, who had risen from his tax booth at a single word and left everything to follow, wrote for our own people, showing how Jesus fulfilled all the law and the prophets, how He was the son of David and the son of Abraham, the King of the Jews. And Luke, the beloved physician who had traveled with Paul and stayed with him to the end, made careful inquiry of those of us who had been eyewitnesses from the beginning, and set down an orderly account, that his reader might have certainty concerning the things he had been taught; and then he wrote a second book, of the acts of the apostles, that the story might be carried on past the empty tomb into the spreading of the word through all the world.

I gave my own testimony where and when I could, for I had promised myself, on the day the cloud took Him from our sight, that I would spend whatever was left of my life telling what I had seen. And it is a strange and holy thing, in my old age, to watch the story that I lived become Scripture—to know that the very words a frightened band of fishermen and tax collectors had spoken in fear, behind locked doors, would be read aloud in every nation under heaven, in every tongue, as the very word of God, exactly as the Lord had said the gospel would be proclaimed to all the world before the end should come. The witnesses were passing, one after another, into glory; but the witness would remain. The seed we had been given to scatter had become a tree in whose branches the nations of the earth were finding their rest.

It has been a strange grace of my old age to watch the very things I lived become Scripture, to know that words spoken by frightened fishermen behind locked doors are now read aloud as the word of God in lands whose names we never knew. I gave my testimony where I could, and others wrote, each as the Lord moved him, and I have marveled at how the same Lord shines through them all, each telling truly what he saw and heard. I think often that the Lord arranged it so on purpose: that the gospel should rest not on the word of one man, who might be doubted, but on a cloud of witnesses who saw the same risen Christ and could not be silenced. We did not invent Him; we could not have. Frightened men do not die for tales they have made up. We told what we had seen, and the telling has outlived us all, and will outlive every empire, for the word of the Lord endures forever.
§§ The Gospel of John

The years went on, and one by one the old companions went home to the Lord, until at last, of those who had walked with Him by the lake of Galilee, only a very few remained, and then fewer still. John lived longest of the twelve, an old man at Ephesus, gentle and unwearied, returning always to his one great theme, which was love. And in his old age he wrote his own account of the Lord—not as the others had written, beginning with the manger or the baptism, but reaching back behind the beginning of all things: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through Him, and without Him was not anything made that was made. In Him was life, and the life was the light of men. And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen His glory, glory as of the only Son from the Father, full of grace and truth."

When I first heard those words read, I wept for joy, for it was the deepest and truest thing that any of us had ever managed to say about the Man we had followed through the dust of Galilee. That the carpenter from Nazareth, whose tired feet I had watched gather the dust of the roads, who had slept in our boats and eaten at our tables and wept at our friend's tomb, was the eternal Word, God Himself, the maker of all things, come down and made flesh to dwell among us—that the glory we had beheld on the mountain and at the empty tomb was the glory of the only Son of the Father. John gathered up the signs we had seen, the water made wine and the bread multiplied and Lazarus called from the grave, and the great sayings of the Lord, the bread of life, the light of the world, the good shepherd, the resurrection and the life, the way and the truth and the life, the true vine. And he told plainly why he had set it all down: "These are written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in His name." Life in His name—the very thing Peter had cried before the council long ago, that there is salvation in no other name under heaven. John had written the whole of his Gospel to one end: that whoever read it might believe and live.

When I first heard John's opening words read aloud—"In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was God... and the Word became flesh and dwelt among us"—I had to stop and weep, for he had said the thing the rest of us had circled around for years without quite daring to say so plainly. We had followed a man; we had watched Him eat and sleep and weep and bleed; and that man was God, the eternal Word, the maker of all things, come down and clothed in our flesh. I had touched Him; John had leaned on His breast at the supper; and He was the One by whom the worlds were made. It is a thing too great for the mind to hold, and yet it is the very center of everything: that God did not save us from a distance, sending help down from heaven, but came Himself, in person, into our dust and our death, to seek and to save us with His own hands and His own blood. The Word became flesh. There is no deeper truth than that, and no greater comfort.
§§ The Letters of John

John wrote letters too in those last long years, and they returned again and again, like a tide, to two things: the love of God, and the blood of His Son. He had stood at the foot of the cross, the one disciple who had not fled, and had watched with his own eyes the blood and water flow from the Lord's pierced side; and to the very end of his long life he could not stop telling sinners that there was cleansing in that blood for all who would come. "If we walk in the light, as He is in the light," he wrote, "we have fellowship with one another, and the blood of Jesus His Son cleanses us from all sin." And he would not let any soul despair: "If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness." And again, for those who stumbled: "If anyone does sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous; and He is the propitiation for our sins, and not for ours only but also for the sins of the whole world."

But the word that rang through all his letters, the word he had learned, I think, by leaning on the Lord's own breast at the supper and by standing beneath His cross, was love. "See what kind of love the Father has given to us," he wrote, "that we should be called children of God; and so we are." And: "In this is love, not that we have loved God but that He loved us and sent His Son to be the propitiation for our sins." And, simplest of all, the deepest thing the old man could say after a lifetime of following: "God is love." He had seen the proof of it with his own eyes, lifted up and bleeding on a Roman cross, and he spent the last of his days telling the world that the love which made the stars had come down and given itself for sinners, and that whoever would believe in the Son had eternal life, and that we love because He first loved us.

That John, after a whole long lifetime of following the Lord, came at the last to so simple a word, that God is love, has always seemed to me the ripe fruit of everything. He had begun, like the rest of us, full of fire and ambition, a son of thunder who wanted to call down flame on a village that would not receive the Lord. And he ended an old man whose every letter circled back to love: love one another; God is love; we love because He first loved us. That is what a lifetime in the presence of Christ does to a man, if he will let it: it burns away the thunder and leaves the love. And John had seen the proof of that love with his own eyes, for he was the one disciple who did not flee, who stood beneath the cross and watched the blood and water flow from the pierced side. He knew what the love of God looked like, for he had seen it lifted up and bleeding, and he spent his last breath telling the world.
§§ Revelation: The Lamb on the Throne

Last of all came the great vision. In the days of a new persecution under Caesar, John, now very old, was exiled to a small and rocky island called Patmos in the sea, for the word of God and the testimony of Jesus. And there, on the Lord's day, the Lord met His aged servant once more, and gave him to see the end of the whole story. When his account of it at last reached the churches, I read it as a man reads the final page of a book that he has lived inside his whole life long, and found that the ending was greater than anything I had dared to hope.

John saw the Lord again—no longer the bound and bleeding prisoner of Pilate's hall, nor the broken figure on the cross, but the risen and glorified Christ in blazing majesty, His face like the sun shining in full strength, His voice like the roar of many waters, holding in His hand the keys of Death and Hades, and saying, "Fear not, I am the first and the last, and the living one. I died, and behold I am alive forevermore, and I have the keys of Death and Hades." And John was caught up in the Spirit into heaven itself, and saw the throne of God, and around it the worship of all the living creatures and the elders; and then, in the midst of the throne, he saw a Lamb standing, as though it had been slain. A Lamb—still bearing the marks of slaughter, the wounds upon it—standing alive at the very center of all the glory of heaven; and the whole of creation fell down before it and sang a new song: "Worthy is the Lamb who was slain, to receive power and wealth and wisdom and might and honor and glory and blessing!" I have wept over that page more than any other in all the Scriptures, for it gathered up into one everything I had seen and everything I had hoped. The Lamb of God whom John the Baptist had pointed out by the muddy waters of the Jordan on the very first day, the Lamb led silently to the slaughter, the Passover Lamb whose blood was the ransom of the world—there He was at the last, at the center of the universe, slain and yet standing, His wounds now His eternal glory, worshiped forever by all that lives as the One who alone was worthy, and worthy precisely because He was slain.

And John saw why the Lamb was counted worthy. They sang to Him a new song: "Worthy are you to take the scroll and to open its seals, for you were slain, and by your blood you ransomed people for God from every tribe and language and people and nation, and you have made them a kingdom and priests to our God, and they shall reign on the earth." From every nation. The thing I had first glimpsed at a Samaritan well, that had broken open at Cornelius' house, that had run through Antioch and Athens and Corinth and Rome and out to the very ends of the earth—here it was at the end, complete and gathered home: a great multitude that no one could number, from every nation and tribe and people and tongue, standing before the throne and before the Lamb, clothed in white robes and with palm branches in their hands, crying out with a loud voice, "Salvation belongs to our God who sits on the throne, and to the Lamb!" And one of the elders explained to John who they were and how their robes were made white: "These are the ones coming out of the great tribulation. They have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb." White robes, washed clean in blood—the great exchange that Paul had written of, the sinner clothed in a righteousness not his own, shown now as the eternal dress of the whole company of the redeemed, in the light of the throne.

I have read that vision until I know it by heart, and the part that undoes me every time is this: that when John looked to see the Lion of Judah who had conquered, he saw instead a Lamb, standing as though it had been slain. The conqueror is a slain Lamb. The marks of the slaughter are not hidden in heaven, nor healed away as though they had never been; they are His eternal glory, the very reason all creation falls down and sings that He is worthy. I had stood beneath the cross and seen those wounds made; I had touched the print of them in the risen body; and now I learn that they will shine at the center of heaven forever, the trophies of the victory by which He bought us. We shall not forget, through all eternity, what it cost Him to save us, for we shall see the wounds and worship. The Lamb who was slain is worthy—worthy precisely because He was slain—and that song will never end.
§§ Revelation: All Things New

John saw the long judgment of all the enemies of God, the defeat of the dragon and the beast and the false prophet, and the last judgment before the great white throne, where the dead were judged by what was written in the books, and death and Hades themselves were thrown at last into the lake of fire. And then he saw the thing toward which the whole story had been straining since the gates of Eden were shut behind our first parents: a new heaven and a new earth, for the first heaven and the first earth had passed away, and the sea was no more; and the holy city, the new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband. And he heard a loud voice from the throne saying the words that are the end and the crown of all the gospel: "Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man. He will dwell with them, and they will be His people, and God Himself will be with them as their God. He will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more, neither shall there be mourning nor crying nor pain anymore, for the former things have passed away."

No more death. The last enemy, the one I had watched the Lord defeat at the gate of Nain and at the bedside of Jairus' little girl and at the tomb of Lazarus, and at last and forever in His own rising on the third morning—abolished now, swallowed up in victory, cast into the lake of fire, never to touch the redeemed again. No more tears, no more mourning, no more pain; the curse undone, the long exile ended, the Father's house thrown open, and God dwelling with His people face to face. And He who was seated on the throne said, "Behold, I am making all things new." John saw the city need no temple, for its temple is the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb; and it had no need of sun or moon, for the glory of God gave it light, and its lamp was the Lamb; and the leaves of the tree of life were for the healing of the nations, and there would be no more anything accursed, and His servants would see His face, and reign forever and ever.

No more death. I have read those words over the graves of nearly everyone I loved, and I read them now as my own end draws near, and they are the sweetest words outside the gospel itself, for they are the gospel's final fruit. The last enemy, the one I watched the Lord defeat at Nain and at Jairus' bedside and at the tomb of Lazarus and at last in His own rising, is to be abolished forever, cast into the lake of fire, never again to touch one of the redeemed. And with it go the tears and the mourning and the pain and the whole long curse that has lain upon the world since Eden. God Himself will dwell with His people and wipe every tear from their eyes with His own hand. This is what the whole story was always moving toward, from the first promise in the garden to the Lamb upon the throne: not merely that our sins should be forgiven, great as that is, but that God should dwell with man, face to face, forever, and make all things new. I have watched the sky a long time for that day. It is nearer now than it has ever been.
§§ The Last Word

I am very old now, older than I ever thought to be, and I have outlived nearly all who walked those dusty roads with me. My hands shake as I set these final things down, and my eyes are dim, but the memory is as bright in me as the morning each thing happened. I have told it all, from the first day to the last—from the day John the Baptist pointed across the Jordan and cried, "Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world," to the day John on Patmos saw that same Lamb standing slain and glorious at the very center of heaven, worshiped by every nation that He had bought with His own blood. And I have come to see, looking back across the whole long sweep of it, that it is all one story, and that it has only ever been about one thing: how God came down to seek and to save the lost, and would not stop—not at the manger, not at the cross, not at the empty tomb, not at Pentecost, not at the ends of the earth, not at the fall of the holy city, and not until He has gathered in His own from every nation, and wiped away every tear, and made all things new.

I think now of the men I knew. I think of Peter, who denied Him by the fire and was restored by another fire, and who followed Him at last to a cross of his own. I think of Stephen, the first of us to fall, his face like an angel's, praying for his murderers as the stones fell. I think of Saul, the worst of our enemies, struck blind on the Damascus road and made the greatest of the heralds, the chief of sinners who never got over being forgiven. I think of Lydia by the river, and the jailer trembling with his sword, and the Ethiopian rejoicing in his chariot, and the multitude no man can number. And in every one of them I see the same hand at work that found me by the Jordan when I was young and thought that I was finding Him—the seeking, saving, sovereign mercy of God, that lays hold of the unworthy and the unwilling and the dead, and will not let them go.

The vision John received closes with a promise and a prayer, and I can find no better words to end my own account than the ones the Spirit gave him. The Lord says, "Surely I am coming soon." And the church, the whole great company of the ransomed—the prodigals brought home, the dead raised to life, the sinners clothed in white, the nations gathered around the throne—answers Him with one voice across all the years and all the lands: "Amen. Come, Lord Jesus." So I lay down my pen, and I wait, and I watch the sky, as I have watched it since the cloud first took Him from the Mount of Olives. The light that drew me to Him by the river on the first day has never once gone out in all the years since; it burns brighter than ever now, at the very end of my days, and soon—soon—I shall see His face again, and the wounds in His hands, and I shall know fully, even as I have been fully known. Until that day, I tell what I have seen, that whoever reads it may believe; and that believing, he may have life in His name.

And if any who read this should ask what they must do to share in all that I have told, how they too may be washed in the blood of the Lamb and stand at last among that countless multitude before the throne, I will give them the same answer the apostles gave the trembling jailer, the same answer that saved the dying thief, the same that found me by the Jordan when I was young: believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved. Not by your works, not by your worthiness, not by any goodness of your own, for you have none that will stand, and neither had I. Only come to Him as you are, a sinner with empty hands, and trust the One who came to seek and to save the lost. He turned away no one who came to Him in all the years I walked beside Him, and He turns away no one still. The door He opened with His own torn flesh stands open yet. Come in, before the night falls, and you too shall see His face, and know, as I am soon to know, that He is faithful who promised.
